en: [Of Kavirāja Vākpatirāja] [p. 1] [of Kavirāja Vākpatirāja]
[Gauḍavaho] [Gauḍavaddha] [Auspicious Invocation]
First, bow to the Self-born (Brahmā), who is like the white lotus of the celestial garden, having emerged from the belly of Hari with its stalk and fibers cast out;
he whose broad seed was concealed within the womb of the navel-ring. (Gauḍavaho 1) [Āryā] He is victorious.
Bow down to Him who dwells within the lotus of the heart— which is like a treasure-chest filled with many sacred vessels—
as He resides there under the guise of the *tiṅgicchī* flower, having undertaken the creation of the worlds like a collection of atoms. (Gauḍavaho 2–3)

Victory to him for whom the sequence of Brahmā’s eggs serves as a row of crystal beads for his necklace, while the eight worlds whirl around like a lotus fiber-root sprouting from the vast serpent Śeṣa situated below.
Pay homage to him who emerges from the sprouts of the lotus-stalks of the great Śeṣa situated beneath.

Victory to the deer, whose fawn-like hue rests gracefully in playful repose within the courtyard of the world filled with water from the broad orb of the moon— like a blue lotus emerging from black mud that has been broken open. (Gauḍavaha 5–6)

Victorious is the Lion among Men, the hero who supports the sky with the smoke spreading from the destruction of the bones of the Asuras, appearing like a mass of clouds seized by the roar of his wrath. (Gaüḍavaho 7) [Āryā meter]
Bow down to him, under whom the arms of the Daityas—though they had shattered the vault of the sky and spread wide—found no resolution against his chest when he descended;
bow down to him who made the horizons of the sky blossom with the blood of the lord of the Danavas after he had deliberated upon it. (Gauḍavaho 8) [Āryā]
Like the evening twilight extended at the time of the river’s flow, he is like a lion for the elephant of Madhumatha.

(Gaüḍavaho 9) Even though his status as a leader of men has been relinquished, the speech of Hari—whose throat is choked with roars—victoriously resounds for a long time with the deep rumbling of laughter. (Gaüḍavaho 10)
The fury of the illusory Māyāmataiṇda arises only from the Asura, who delights in the mass of clouds fleeing like deer from the moon of the disregarded Diṅgāga;
he is like a dense, supportless cluster of lightning flashes shattered by the roar of his wrath. (Gauḍavaho 11) [Āryā]
Victorious is the man-lion with his tawny mane, the very ornament of the neck!
Victorious is he who, in the state of a cowherd, bears a fragrance that issues forth from his pure and hidden lotus-like navel, even as it flows through his gentle breaths.
The tusk of the Great Boar, having emerged through the path of his mouth, triumphs like a lotus stalk with its root from the navel-lotus residing within his belly. (Gaüḍavaho 13) [Āryā] [p.
Bow down to him who, while in the state of a lowly beast, bore the earth—though it rested upon Śeṣa—as if it were reflected in the jewels of his hoods through the transmission of his majesty;
carrying it like a parasol below to ward off the sun standing above. (Gauḍavaho 14) [Āryā]

The earth, far removed from the breath of the Boar, goes forth with the moon as its crest. (Gaüḍavaha 15) In Vāmana’s dwarf form, Viṣṇu’s limbs appear like unevenly sized earthen mounds, as if they were barely sufficient to fill the worlds contained within his small belly. (Gaüḍavaha 16)

May the line of hair on the belly of the Slayer of Madhu protect you— [that line] which, like a great tortoise supporting the earth with its five-clawed trunk, upholds the world by means of his body, having cast off the burden from the tips of his mouth. (Gauḍavaho 17) [Āryā metre]
Like a swarm of bees following a lotus with its stalk hidden within,
he is victorious— he in whose youth a certain majesty emerged from his waist and hips, as the worlds grew thin and paled with envy. (Gauḍavaho 18–19)
He who wears a forest garland, which has a swarm of bees at its face like a swarm of bees at the mouth of a drunkard, is like the inner apartment of the residence of Lakṣmī. (Gauḍavaho 20) [Āryā] [p.

In her childhood, Hariṇī won the kiss upon Yaśodā’s face, which was like a white lotus emerging from the path of the navel that had been forbidden; may the lines of her nails, appearing like the form of Rāhu, grant you compassion and aesthetic delight. (Gauḍavaho 21) [Āryā] May they [the nail-marks] protect you.
Salute that [neck] of Kṛṣṇa, which, even today, as it shines with the rays of the Kaustubha jewel upon its chest,
causes Rāhu— who has had his throat severed— to experience an inconceivable suffering through breaths that are shallow and rootless. (Gauḍavaho 22–23)
Bow down to the feet of Bala, whose dark upper garments—the effects of pride and vice—have become loosened as if the Yamunā were being churned by the fear of his roar;
they seem to emit the luster of the thousands of jewels from the hoods retracted within. (Gauḍavaho 24) [Āryā meter]
May the glance of Hari, which dispels the darkness of ignorance, destroy your misfortunes.
Victorious is the playful stride of Balarāma and Keśava, who, because their power is self-evident, leave the remaining tortoises crushed under the weight [of their steps], rendering them supportless.
Bow down to that one who, out of passion, bears a body naturally dark-complexioned, variegated as if by the alternating emergence and departure of day and night. (Gauḍavaho 27) [Āryā] [p.
The paths leading to the breasts of Śrī, emerging from her parted body and appearing like lotus petals upon her chest, proceed toward the bee-like face of Madhumathana.
Victorious is he, upon whose forehead the line of his eyebrows clings to his eyes.
Even today, it appears like the bow of Kāma, blackened by the heat of his fire.

Bow down to him, O you who love Kāma, who even now supports the moon bound with matted locks, as if it were the moon that had undertaken the task of falling into the fire of his third eye. (Gauḍavaho 29–30)
May he bring you happiness, whose forehead dwells upon his head under the guise of the moon—[the forehead] struck by the wide, tawny eyes [of the Goddess].
May he who, under the guise of a bow tawny with a cluster of drawn flowers, conquers... [Śiva]. (Gauḍavaho 31) [Āryā metre]
As if having rushed forward and been swallowed by her third eye, Kāma was consumed by her; [thus it is said].
(Gaüḍavaho 32) I bow perpetually to that which, illuminated by the moonlight of the crescent moon resting upon the lap of the crown, possesses the white splendor of a dwarf. (Gaüḍavaho 33)
Victorious is he whose arms, crowded with armlets, bracelets, and golden ornaments, bear the scars of wounds from the bow-staffs of Bāṇa, like two sighs of indignation. (Gauḍavaho, Āryā) [p.
Bow to the eye of the enemy of Andhaka, its pupil aflame,
raised upward like the upraised discus of Viṣṇu when his arrow was broken;
victorious is the hand of the wielder of the Pināka bow, even though it has a matted lock of hair, yet is grasped by a serpent.
Victorious is Hara, who, bowing at the feet of the enraged Umā, has his crest-jewel tossed up in haste;
he rolls about amidst the rays of the jewels on her long, matted locks, as if out of fear that his head might touch the skull of Brahmā resting upon it. (Gauḍavaho, Āryā verses D and E)

Bow down to him, whose waters—even today—flow crookedly due to the breaking of the three paths, as if made uneven by the arrangement of his matted locks; he who, at the cessation of the churning of the ocean, performed the binding of the matted locks of the Lord of Beasts (Śiva).
Victory to the binding of the matted locks of the Lord of Beasts (Śiva), which ceased when the churning of the ocean was finished.
With his chest weary from rubbing against the mountain slopes, he has a pale complexion;
with his forehead reddened by the pressure of fingers trembling in a fit of anger, he bows to Hara’s Kirāta form, as if forbidding the emergence of a third eye. (Gauḍavaho 34–35)

He dies instantly, his throat marked by lines that fade as they are drawn and turned away in a moment, like the scratches of a snake’s coils when its venom has been swallowed all at once. (Gauḍavaho 36) [Āryā] [p.

Bow down to him who still bears upon his head the third eye, which remained fixed there even after somehow slipping from it, like a flower placed upon the forehead of a maiden. Victorious is he whose throat-base is adorned by the mass of matted locks of the world of the upper regions (the heavens).
Like a streak of lead, possessing the luster of poison, is the line upon Śiva’s throat.
Bow to the three-eyed moon, which remains in a state of fragmentation as if its sole heart were devoted to the worship of Gaurī, who occupies half of his body. (Gauḍavaho 38–39)
Bow down to him whose forehead, like a moon joined with a creeper, long drank the stream of the celestial river from his skull as if from a gentle dawn.
Bow down to the Eye of the Pināka-wielder, whose brow-eye has shimmering reddish-brown pupils.
Even today, he is like a mass of burning embers that has been swallowed;
bow down to him, for even now the bodiless Kāma, avoiding that family as if it were his own kin, does not abandon fear toward Kumāra. (Gauḍavaho 41–42)
Victorious is she by whose ankleted foot the shoulder of the demon Mahiṣāsura was struck, causing a shower of blood to burst forth like blossoms. (Gauḍavaho 43) [Āryā] [p.

May the eyes of the noble lady, whose strength was somewhat diminished as she leaned upon her neck during their first embrace and felt bashful, grant you happiness. (Gaüḍavaha 44) [Āryā meter] The Great Goddess Mahākālī has wandered through the various skulls at the time of universal destruction.

Like the many fragments of the moon scattered across hundreds of thousands of nights of the full dark fortnight—may Cāmuṇḍā’s body protect you; her body, which is swollen from the bursting of the veins on her broad neck and filled with the bracelets that have overflowed from her small waist. (Gauḍavaha 45–46)
She, who sports in the lotus-petal-like laps of the four-faced Brahmās and whose feet are placed upon the masses of the tongues of poets, wanders about;
bow down to that moon whose orb appears with the luster of a spotless mark. *Gaüḍavaha* 47. [Āryā]
Salute that Vairūṭya mine, whose beauty is as if emptied from the middle by the waters flowing out from the Gaṅgā;
for its chariot-horses carry it away like steeds that have just on that very day driven off the filth of darkness. (Gauḍavaho 48–49)

That which shines forth as a mass for the protection of the world at the time of sunrise, and that dense mass of rays which spreads out at the time of the sun’s setting—[this is the cowherd]. (Gauḍavaho 50) [Āryā;

Bow down to him who, in his weighing of the Kola tree, bears the circle of the earth—lightened by being divided among his many heads—as if it were reflected in the jewels of all the hoods; he who bears the stream of the celestial river as if it were a staff made of the waters of the Yamunā.
(Gauḍavaho 51) [Āryā metre] Pay homage to him who holds the flow of the divine river as if it were a pillar fashioned from the water of the Kālindī.
Bow down to that elephant-faced one, whose trunk is like a pillar of ivory and whose hand is wide;
he who, in the playful sport of his broad tusk-trunks, makes the slopes of Mount Meru appear as if the Himavat and Vindhya mountains have merged together. (Gauḍavaho 52–53)

Victorious is the smile of the Lord of the Gaṇas, which—like a collection of teeth—is smeared with the red lac of his love for Gaurī clinging to him during their sleep, and which appears like a mass of teeth piled upon the left half of his face.
Salutations to the son of Madhu, who brought about the destruction of the lord of the Daityas, as he approached... [Gaüḍavaho 54, Āryā metre]
The playful tremblings of pride have been made to wander by Lakṣmī.
(Gaüḍavaha 55) Victory to her who has emerged with lotuses and the moon held in her hands—Śrī, as it were, having surpassed the quality of the beauty of her own face. (Gaüḍavaha 56)

Bow down to him who holds in his hand the bow of flowers and arrows of bees clinging to it—his hand being like the collyrium-mark on the forehead of Rati, who has been made to weep by the God of Love. (Gauḍavaho 57) [Āryā] [p.

May that Ganges bring you happiness, she who—like a white silk scarf slipping from the heads of the lords of beasts (the elephants) when they are distressed by the heat—whirls around the lap of Himālaya as if to support it;
she who, with her skull-cup whirling in her water, dwells upon the head of Hara. (Gaüḍavaho 58) [Āryā meter]
Even today, the four-faced Brahmā bears the stainless mark of the toenails of the Lord.
The first face has been washed, as it were, by the luster of the toenails of Hari; the second has been joined, as it were, by the feet of Hara’s moon. (Gauḍavaho 59–60)
Bow to the water of the Gaṅgā, which has assumed the white luster of snow upon its encounter with the moon, as if it were purified by its very cause. (Gaüḍavaho 61) [Āryā] [p.
[Now, the Praise of Poets:

Here, those poets are truly born who can perceive this entire world as it exists within their words—whether it appears as something substantial like a mass of clouds or as something trivial. (Gauḍavaho 62) [Āryā meter]

Those great poets who, by their own speech alone, instill dignity in themselves and attain praise here, find happiness even in misfortune and transform their wealth into the alleviation of suffering. (Gaüḍavaho 63) [Āryā]
The hearts of those who delight in the ultimate essence of poetry are won over. [Gaüḍavaha 64, Āryā] Beauty blossoms for Prakrit when its words are adorned with Sanskrit;
likewise, through the excellence of Sanskrit, Prakrit also attains power. [Gaüḍavaha 65, Āryā]
The boneless appears as if it has bones, the bony seems as if it were scattered, and things appear exactly as they are situated—such are the innate qualities of good poets.
Just as modesty and the majesty of the scepter adorn the glory of a king, so do these qualities adorn the poetry of the great. (Gauḍavaho 66) [Āryā metre]
Likewise, the tinkling sound and sweetness of the speech enhance one another.
(Gaüḍavaho 67) Even a mere fragment of the Goddess of Fortune, when being praised, shines and brings delight;
but what can Sarasvatī do when she is incomplete? (Gaüḍavaho 68)

How indeed could the speech of women, already occupied with the sport of love, be silenced by this [spring], which is like a delicate second flower appearing after the first flowers of the forest creepers? (Gaüḍavaho 69) [Āryā]
A good person will not be attached to the blame spoken by the wicked;

however, for them, that blame becomes consolidated through the fault of their own disparagement of the good. (Gaüḍavaho 70) [Āryā meter] Through a succession of concealing the virtues of others, they become experts in perceiving those very virtues as faults.
By those very virtues, the virtuous become even more objects of malice for the wicked;
alas, that even stainless ones are distressed by the spotless virtues of the good is comparable to the pain of an elephant’s tusk being struck by the rays of the moon. (Gauḍavaho 71–72)
Know that blame is brought about by those who are partial; praise and blame alike are brought about by them. That which is brought about by such does not trouble one who is free from pride.
May they rejoice in the weight of their own virtues, having never seen the reflection on the faces of others. (Gauḍavaho 73) [Āryā]
The faces of others, seen while he was swinging on the swing of his own virtue, were made to bloom by him, who was heavy with dignity.

(Gaüḍavaha 74) Although the world attained fame through the mere possession of many common virtues, it is only because of him that the title "common poet" (*sāmaṇṇa-kai*) became established. (Gaüḍavaha 75)

Even though its nature is beautiful, what excellence can shine forth when it has entered dull matter? Even the reflection of the sun, situated in water, shines with its face turned downwards. (Gaüḍavaha Gāthā)

Even a minute quality of another captivates when one’s own qualities are heavy; for contentment with one's own virtues is the very essence of character and discernment. Even other qualities shine forth when they first encounter the company of the great. (Gauḍavaho 76) [Āryā]
Like moonbeams falling upon a mountain peak, they were foremost on the earth.
(Gaüḍavaho 77) As they bestow complete auspiciousness and every means of welfare, something indescribable emerges from them such that even they themselves are filled with wonder. (Gaüḍavaho 78)
How could one who possesses the qualities not be free from pride, when there is the forest of their very absence?
Those who desire virtue and seek the goal of virtue do not harbor arrogance, for they have transcended the world and abide in oneness as the great ones. (Gauḍavaho 79) [Āryā meter]
Envy, throbbing with jealousy, depends upon whom it regards as its object.

(Gaüḍavaha 80) Those for whom the very doubt of their own intellect becomes the basis for further intellectual inquiry—those whose nature is thus established do not exist in this world. (Gaüḍavaha 81)
Through the joy of empty knowledge, the arrogant display of the wicked succeeds; through the suffering of the virtuous, their hearts tremble. (Gaüḍavaho, Āryā)

Those whose names are well-established in their own compositions—surely both their completion and their creation have been achieved by Sukaī. For in their poetry, garlands of syllables possess a life of their own. (Gaüḍavaho I, Āryā)

...those very qualities of the living being continue to exist even when it has died. (Gauḍavaho J, Āryā) Is life for those whose virtues have ascended to the heights of joy? For even when a man of merit is praised by them, he is not believed as such, as if his virtues had acquired a treacherous nature. (Gauḍavaho K, Āryā)
That [consciousness], though insentient, is awakened by the Great One (the Self) for the purpose of its own awakening;
through the transmission of that awakening, it assumes its own true nature as if by itself.
He who perceives his own essence also desires that of another.
Even he who adopts the qualities of others... is also to be pitied. (Gaüḍavaho M [Āryā]) Among those established as virtuous, there are only two types;
and even that [second type] is considered inferior if he possesses only a mediocre disposition. (Gaüḍavaho N [Āryā])

Who can censure one who is exceedingly grave in his own nature? Who is able to praise the state of equanimity toward both those who have been praised and those who have been reviled? (Gaüḍavaho 82) [Āryā metre]

Those who, having heard, understand the supreme [truth] and do not waver even within themselves—how do they not feel ashamed before the haughty ones who are like the sun? (Gaüḍavaho 83) [Āryā meter]. The qualities of Time were first explored by the poets upon paths that are beyond grasp.
Otherwise, some people find it difficult to carry out even a small portion of what is desired by others.
(Gaüḍavaha 84) How indeed could there be anything undesirable in paths frequented by poets?
But when that boundary is abandoned, everything becomes truly new once again. (Gaüḍavaha 85)
The emergence of qualities is difficult for those of dull intellect;
it is not that the sky is blue, but rather the cessation of the eye's luminosity.
The intellects of other poets wander, flickering as they seek out meaning. (Gauḍavaho, Āryā)

Indeed, the hearts of the monkey-kings are devoid of any undertaking. (Gauḍavaho 86) Even today, the movement of words—whose essence was grasped by the foremost of monkeys from the very beginning of saṃsāra—triumphs as if still fresh and innocent. (Gauḍavaho 87)
[16] Why have even those excellent poets, whose minds were focused on nothing else, studied this speech until it became the very essence of their extraordinary nature? (Gauḍavaho 88) [Āryā metre]
Who can describe the detailed expansion of those [great ones] who remain in the world?

For even when their names alone have been transmitted, the qualities of the great shine forth as if manifest. Even others become somewhat proud upon merely understanding their true nature. (Gauḍavaho 89) [Āryā]
They carry the majesty of their own speech, which is unsurpassed; (Gaüḍavaho 90).
By causing both delusion and awakening, it conquers the net of conflicting doubts of the lords of poets, like darkness or like light; (Gaüḍavaho 91).
The ninth treasure is vision; the coolness of its arrangement is the power of composition.
This unceasing flow of poetic excellence extends here throughout the entire world, reaching even to the very foot of the mountain.
Those works which are, as it were, empty, appearing in many places with only a sparse essence of merit—*Gaüḍavaha*, 92. [Āryā]
What is the use of those compositions which merely follow the ancient rules of grammar?
Only those poetic reputations are truly fashioned,
whose fame enters the ears of the world, dwells in its heart, and spreads across its face.
[17] But even so,
they cling to the heart, just as women who are delightful by their very disposition [cling to] lovers,
and as the utterances of great poets [cling to] the hearts of those who love them. (Gaüḍavaho, Āryā)
The winds enter this ocean and from here they depart;
the winds come from the ocean and carry away only the waters of the sea.
[Gaüḍavaho 93] [Āryā meter] There is a particular joy that causes the eyes to bloom and yet causes them to close.

Now, externally turned inward, it expands within my heart. (Gaüḍavaha 94) Compassion, or even tears, or perhaps the disregard shown by the great toward others who possess ignoble qualities—these may occur; but never the suffering of the heart. (Gaüḍavaha 95)
Even if they are not equal to oneself, what does it matter what such people say?

Even those who desire to surpass others in whatever way still show great respect to the venerable. Let them be free from pride, or let them act with their greatness exalted. (Gaüḍavaho 96) [Āryā meter]

In whatever way their virtues manifest, they do not become an object of ridicule for the world. (Gaüḍavaho 97) In this world, the heart may be as if terrified, or ashamed; as if paralyzed with pride, or as if exhausted;
as if distressed, or as if overwhelmed with joy. (Gaüḍavaho 98)
[Page 18] Now, the poem begins:
There is one who gladdens Mahinda by having averted all the misfortunes of the world.
The lord of the earth named Śrī Yaśodharman, whose virtues were grasped by every quarter, stirs the earth into the state of dust as he moves;
rising up, it swirls like a white whirlwind that has not abandoned its remaining coils. (Gauḍavaho 99–100)

Even today, the braided tresses of his captive enemies remain curled, though their bosoms have been abandoned by necklaces that— distressed by the suffering of separation— seem to flee from the blows of their hands. (Gauḍavaho 5)

They appear like the tracks of fingers pressed deep by a firm pulling. (Gauḍavaho 100) When he moves, Śeṣa does not release his grip on the circle of the earth, though his hoods are spread wide with pain;
for he is pinned down by the weight of the earth’s circumference, his jewels sunk deep. (Gauḍavaho 101)

In the battles, his sword—its edge slightly reddened by the fire of the anger of the slain, as if smeared with the ichor of elephants—drips [blood]. In firm prostrations, their foreheads become circles joined by palms held in service. (Gauḍavaho 102) [Āryā]
He whose rival feudatories are like the contraction of a frown cast down;
he who, at the moment of exertion, glances slightly with pride toward his right shoulder.
He makes the Goddess of Fortune, who dwells upon his arm, joyful through the grace of his vision.
(Gaüḍavaho 104) The foreheads of the captives of his enemies become calm, as if turbid with the shifting glints of light from their uneven pupils due to their state of agitation.
(Gaüḍavaho 105)
In the presence of the illustrious Pārvatīluṅkhia, the great forest of his enemies appears like a mass of shadows fallen upon a massive tree.
(Gauḍavaha 106) Deep and grand in its undertakings, it roams about as if having conceived the ocean itself.
He for whom Bhāratī is like the river Bhāgīrathī flowing through other worlds;
And he for whom the quarters of the sky, brushed by thousands of streams of ichor from the elephants of the turning world and where fly-whisks are moved in agitation, seem to run away.

Moreover— her lower lip shines, its surface uneven with the slight protrusion of the tooth-sockets, which are pressed forward as the tips of her fingers are withdrawn and loosened. (Gaüḍavaha 109) [Āryā]
The sighs, with their filaments slightly trembling and their nectar dripping from the roots, are released silently as they struggle against the play-lotuses. (Gauḍavaho 110) [Āryā;

The auspiciousness of those whose faces are discolored by the play of dejection, their tresses disheveled, crushed, and scattered as they are held up by the left hand, overflows. (Gauḍavaho 111) [Āryā] She smells the bouquet of ornaments consisting of single flowers gathered for the sake of auspiciousness.
His speech, which was honored by the gods who bowed slightly with averted eyes out of reverence,
[is such that] even today the young celestial nymphs— whose amorous play was fashioned by the mere sight of him in battle— suffer in their hearts, as if in silence. (Gauḍavaho 112–113)
Or rather:

The mountains, having reached the sky with the abundance of their peaks and turned back by the bracelets [of light] flashing against the quarters of the horizon, burn as they fall down, finding no space for further movement. (Gauḍavaho 114) [Āryā]

With their flanks embraced by columns of smoke emerging from the mouths of their mountain caves, the mountains—the repositories of the earth—seem to vomit forth molten metal as they are scorched by the fire of thunderbolts; the mass of flame-tips of the fire issuing from their wings is visible as they smolder. (Gauḍavaho 115) [Āryā]
Like the mountain of the gods (Meru), its nights and days moving as it was shaken by the agitation of the battle;
in those very same mountains where the thunderbolt, eager for a violent clash, would be blunted, there alone it was shattered by the counter-attack of the enemy. (Gauḍavaho 116–117)

The mountain ranges, with their vast and wide-open caves appearing like gaping mouths protruding from the interior of the ravines, tremble all at once as if they were pregnant women giving birth out of fear. (Gaüḍavaha 118) [Āryā metre]

The mountain, though remaining fixed in its place, melts like the ocean that has come from all directions out of fear of being encircled by the earth bent under the pressure of the tremors; it is as if the fire of the destruction of its wings were burning within.
On that very day, its ridges were heated by the movement of the solar disc.

The thunderbolt, though it had struck Mount Udayācala, was recognized only after a long time. (Gaüḍavaha 120) The Malaya ridges, whose sandalwood trunks were released by the wind from the fire of the poison-spitting serpents and whose smoke was served by the garments of the gods’ wives, are now being consumed. (Gaüḍavaha 121)
The mountain-crags, with their wings shattered and falling, are crushed upon the earth by the splendor of its petals; at that moment, the serpents flee in agitation as the mountain masses collapse.
Somehow the surface of the earth supports itself, even as it is being struck down by mountains falling with their wings destroyed.
Śeṣa is enraged by the multitude of heads, dripping with blood, torn apart by his fangs.

(Gaüḍavaho 123) The sky is seen as a mountain ablaze, the world of the gods fleeing and turning back from the heat, and the lotus-hand of the Grandfather (Brahmā) smeared with pollen from the lotuses agitated by the smoke. (Gaüḍavaho 124)

Like women sluggish with pregnancy, yet somehow heavy with the burden of their boats hidden in caves, the mountain plateaus once again reach the expanse of the courtyard of the sky. (Gaüḍavaho 125) [Āryā meter]
In the mountain range, which possesses crests of flashing lightning tawny with wings flickering for a moment, the lords of the earth sink like blades of grass;
their breadth diminished, they seem to shrink or to stretch out sparsely. (Gauḍavaho 126) [Āryā metre]

The mountains, though lofty, become thin as their feathers are shattered by the thunderbolt; with their wings stretched out loosely, the mountains—exhausted by the heavy impact of falling as they were struck down by the swiftly hurled vajra—are seized. (Gauḍavaho 127–128)

The thunderbolt strikes the earth; the earth, struck by the falling mountains shattered by the thunderbolt, in turn strikes the circle of Śeṣa’s hoods. The masses of mountains are made bitter by their own smoke, and the feathers of their wings are blown away.
The eyes of the quarters of the sky, as it were, are struck by the rays released from the mountain torrents.
(Gaüḍavaha 130) The ridges of the mountain masses, where the heat has caused the veins of the iron-stone to protrude, have subsequently become suitable for receiving the thunderbolt.
(Gaüḍavaha 131)
Those very mountain torrents, once turbid from the rows of burnt forests, have become like tears mixed with soot for the wives of the mountains who are now filled with sorrow. (Gaüḍavaha 132) [Āryā]

Upon the mountain ridges, long streaks of molten copper are seen, spreading with the smoothness of *saṅkhāa* (vermilion) and resembling the appearance of great serpents fast asleep. The earth’s embrace— its base oozing sap as it is being pressed down from below,
its root loosened by the netherworld’s darkness yet glossy at the tip—
even in a forest where the branches are celestial, it bears the blossoms and fruits of the lord of the groves. (Gaüḍavaho 504) [Āryā meter]

The young tree was cherished by its first bond of affection; likewise, even as evening approached, the day persisted in the city due to the continuous longing for the jewel-like earth and the power of the rising sun. (Gauḍavaho 505–506)

In that region of the city of Harikāntā— which possessed the splendor of a lord’s power, was surrounded by a protective moat, and contained celestial gardens of trees with blossoming fruits— and in that lake of the fame of the great kings who had accepted him according to tradition... [Gaüḍavaho 507] (Āryā meter)
The lord constructed the celestial palace in a single day; its pillar-bases are streaked with the gold of Kṛṣṇa’s armlets. (Gaüḍavaha 508) [Āryā] [p. 78]
Even today, people on the forehead of the mountain have their fingers scarred by stones;
beholding the dark shadow of its peaks, the Lord [Śiva] adopts the guise of a common man among the prosperous inhabitants of that Mandara mountain. (Gauḍavaho 509–510)
As he gradually became absorbed in his task, his splendor— marked by the lord of the yakṣas—
became difficult for others to endure, like the heat of the sun at its zenith. His [sacrificial fires],
fragrant with the flowing resin of fresh *suradāru* wood, were worthy of being honored.
In that region, the breezes were cooled by the intoxicating essence of freshly pressed wine;
moreover, what has come about?—
this lake, whose blossoming water-lilies captivate the heart.
The riverbanks are crowded with water-ranks (cranes) that fill the ponds shimmering within the *nala* thickets. Then,
the mass of water, having crushed the marshes of the netherworld (*pātāla*), bears the luster of the ocean as it meets the sight of the Goddess Śrī residing in the lotus groves.

These regions of the lotus pond have their edges whitened by clusters of lotus petals scattered and tossed about by the wind, while the stalks of the withered, old lotuses remain with their leaves sparse and decayed. (Gaüḍavaha 515) [Āryā;
Here the breeze spreads the fragrance of the *jambū* fruits, which are being plucked by young maidens whose hair is cool with perfume, as well as the honey of the lotuses.
Here, those cranes have their throats made to blossom like tender sprouts by the sweet, soft notes of love. (Gauḍavaho 516) [Āryā metre]
The regions of the dark-blue lotus thickets, licked by the waves, shine brightly.

Here, the essence of the flavor of the breaking waves is divided by drops of water mixed with mud and drawn up through the hollows; it possesses the pungent fragrance of the crushed stalks of lotus fibers.
Here, those forest lotus-pools have their uneven petals densely packed together, thrust out as they emerge one after another;
there, wild cocks stumble as they move about. Here, the cries of ospreys wheeling in the sky break forth, steeped in passion.
In these ponds, the thick lotus petals are struck by fish turning over;
here, the edges of the banks are filled with slimy water-snakes frequented by crows, and where shell-fish and moss have been dragged up by the drying heat. (Gauḍavaho 520–521)
The wind tosses about the lotus leaves here, their bases reddened by the tips of the claws of fighting crabs and slippery with the foam of conch-shells. (Gauḍavaho 522) [Āryā] [p.

The lotus ponds here have their edges salted by the sea, their lofty stalks slightly submerged in water, and their surfaces covered with dense growths of young shoots; these mountains, moreover, with their slopes worn smooth by the constant flow of rivers, bring relief to the weary traveler. (Gaüḍavaho 523) [Āryā metre]
The birds are silent, and the lakes are clear and empty; the forests are serene.
(Gaüḍavaha 524) These rivers have smooth sands bound by circles of mud stirred by waves;
their expanses of banks consist of sparse *kāśa* shoots. (Gaüḍavaha 525)

Here, the villages situated around the edges of the lakes are rarely heard, being drowned out by the clamor of waves made resonant by the cries of intoxicated water-birds. These [villages] possess the first expanse of mud, beautiful from the drying of the full waters.
The marshy thickets, their tips green with fresh sprouts emerging and their locations lush with vegetation, are delightful here at evening;
the cuckoos are vocal as they emerge from the lotus groves, and the grassy plots are fragrant with the scent of slightly warmed mud. (Gauḍavaho 527–528)

Here the paths are variegated with powdered *sambūka* flowers, with smooth white ants' nests polished by friction, and with uneven greenery spreading through the gaps between the branches. (Gauḍavaho 529) [Āryā;
These marshy areas, where the sands at the edges of the slender sleeping reeds are cooled by the fragrance of water trickling from the clusters of *niula* flowers,
carry within their thickets the cries of ospreys intent on catching fish. (Gaüḍavaha 530) [Āryā meter]
Water-leeches, bound with clusters of lotuses smelling of snakes, shine in the young lake;
likewise do the first sprouts, exhausted by the sun, appearing between the crevices of rocks clinging to the mountain slopes. (Gauḍavaho 531–532)
These date-palm groves, their trunks bent by the weight of clusters of ripe, reddish fruit,
and their fruits fragrant with the scent of the slow-moving bees, seem to offer relief to travelers.
Here is that row of *karīra* thickets, tawny with blossoms that curl like manes.
It shines like a mane of a young elephant standing on a whetstone, matted with the fragments of its own hair.

(Gaüḍavaha 534) Here the heart rests, as it were, upon the forest paths fragrant with the breezes from full-blown *phullaka* flowers, where the lotuses are joined by the incoming currents. (Gaüḍavaha 535)
Indeed, because they have been heavily grazed, the village lands do not grow thick with grass;
here, the forest grounds, where the cow dung has turned pale from the drying dew, are preferred. (Gaüḍavaha 536) [Āryā] [p.
These are the hollows of the ponds, where the cow-dung intended for crushing the rows of forest trees has been smeared,
and which are surrounded by water darkened by grey dust. These are the fragrant grounds, covered with wind-grey dung and straw.
The forest clearings, where the cowherd settlements have been abandoned, cause longing.
(Gaüḍavaho 538) Here, the forest borders shine with roots turned green by the emergence of fresh shoots, and with grass grown thick from being grazed upon by wild buffaloes. (Gaüḍavaho 539)

Here, the forest tracts, with their altars for deities inscribed in red ochre, indicate herds of wild buffaloes resting amidst the low-hanging grass; here, jackals prowl through the intervals between the scattered bones of those who have perished. (Gauḍavaho 540) [Āryā]
[The landscape is] filled with the skeletons of buffaloes and crows perched on the quarters of the sky, trembling in fear.
Here, in the ponds, the moonbeams—pale as frost—are like the unevenly curved trunks of elephants, trembling in their thirst for the sun. (Gauḍavaho 541–542)
In this place, the quarters of the sky, soiled by the spray of water droplets from birds flying upward, indicate the direction of the water with breezes cooled by the waves. (Gaüḍavaha 543) [Āryā;
Here, the rivers— whose waters have their surfaces fouled by sands falling from the *kāphukkāra* trees—
are somehow drunk by travelers who are afflicted by the heat of the wind.
(Gaüḍavaho 544) [Āryā meter] Their flow is obstructed by the winds released from the dust raised by the shadows of the trees heated by the sun.
In the evening, the villages here have their fires extinguished as the heat subsides;
this is that forest, with its clusters of straight trees withered by the crushing force of the elephant’s trunk, and its sparse thickets of *śallakī* trees grey with dust. (Gauḍavaha 545–546)

Here is a herd of elephants, whose leaders have turned back their troops with a mere glance of their faces, while the female elephants have retreated because the forest is resonant with the clamor of the gathering bees.
(Gaüḍavaho 547) [Āryā meter] Here, having trampled the ground and lopped off the tops of the nearby *viḍavi* trees, they remain.

The great young herds of elephants are heard trumpeting as they rest here. O hero with mighty thighs, in this place one must wander over lands where wild boars kill each other and where the horns of ruru deer are sparse. (Gauḍavaho 548–549)
Here, in these forest trees whose roots are sparse and which remain only because of the community of wandering sages, the birds feast upon the wild rice fruits. (Gauḍavaha 550) [Āryā;
Here, birds, their flight obstructed by the clusters of trees whose peaks are entwined with dense networks of creepers, ascend into the sky by taking a diagonal path.
Here, even lions shake off the swarms of bees that fly up at their strike.

The forests here captivate the mind with their fresh palāśa blossoms, which are heavy with the nectar-water dripping from the filaments, and which have turned pale as they grow upon the drying ponds. (Gauḍavaho 552–553)
Here, the hollows of the marshy pools— surrounded by palāśa trees cool with droplets of water dripping from crickets,
and possessing sparse kiṃśuka trees standing in the midst of the waterless ground— captivate the heart. On those days, the hard tracks have been formed by the dust driven away by the wind.
In these marshy thickets, the waters are shallow and the ground is strewn with scattered rays of light.
Here, the paths are green with drops of water trickling from the boars as they emerge, while the blades of grass are bent low by the weight of the mud clinging to them. (Gaüḍavaho 555–556)

These ground-surfaces, with their clods of earth crushed by the forceful stamping of hooves and their dust raised by the heaving of the soil, have become thin and parched from being trampled and from the long, rasping sighs of exhaustion. (Gauḍavaha 557) [Āryā] [p.
For here, in the windless forest, the expanse of the sky— its dust-kissed horizon marked by the sighs of elephants— announces the slumber of the herd of cows. [Gaüḍavaho 558,
Āryā meter] Its surface is lowered by the weight of the scattered dust, and its uneven ground is cracked open by fissures.
These slopes of the mountain have branches that are difficult to climb; these plateaus of the mountain are [steep].

(Gaüḍavaho 559) Even though only the trunks remain here, the clusters of trees are recognized by their own great length as being fully capable of acting as fuel for the fire through their state of exhaustion.
(Gaüḍavaho 560)

In this place, the forest—dense with young trees growing in the groves at its edge—steals away the heat of the day by means of its thickets of creepers and vines, providing coolness through the presence of shade; it is a land where the rivers are easily crossed. (Gauḍavaho 561) [Āryā meter] The thick growth of creepers and vines makes the areas of shade cool.
Here are the forests of the Aṇaha, Haladdī, Saddala, Īgiri, and Kaccha mountains.

(Gaüḍavaho 562) In this marshy land, the thickets of leaves—dark and hardened by being trampled every day by the hooves of all the draft oxen—bear a resemblance to the dark, hard-hoofed bands of leather. (Gaüḍavaho 563)
Here is seen the reflection of the sun fallen upon a mass of golden stone rays, reddened by them and as tawny as a ripe, peeled palm fruit. (Gauḍavaho 564) [Āryā] [p.
Here, the streets appear as if covered with drops of sparse water, their royal splendor shattered by the falling of heavy grains of dust raised by the wind.
Here, those [streets] are entirely choked with flowers, leaves, wood, and all manner of debris, moistened at the roots of the trees.
The grounds here are dark blue, covered with withered grass, rough, and strewn with dry dung.

(Gaüḍavaho 566) In this place, there are forest regions where the peacocks are vocal, where the kadamba trees are flowering and variegated with old fruit, and which are cool with palāśa leaves that are double-layered like fruit-cups. (Gaüḍavaho 567)
These trunks of trees, smelling of the ichor rubbed from the temples of the forest elephants and having their bark torn by the claws of lions enraged by them, inspire fear;
here, at evening, they endure the exhaustion of the day, obstructing the sky with heaps of dust. (Gauḍavaho 568) [Āryā metre]
The summer nights have the orb of the moon as their ornament shining in the western quarter;
here, the ponds possess lotus stalks emerging from lotus beds broken by the trampling of herds of elephants, and they abound with lotuses dripping with nectar. (Gauḍavaho 569–570)
Here, the marshy grounds have their banks thick with the fragments of lotus leaves clinging to the trees, while the spaces between the petals are scattered by the wind. (Gauḍavaho 571) [Āryā;
Here, the forests, their roots darkened by the smoke of the forest fires fanned by the wind, shine with the first path of light;
they are valued for their tips of *vāmalūra* plants, tawny from the wind of the fresh fire. (Gauḍavaho 572) [Āryā]
Here, the trees have shed their lower leaves, and the dry lands are fragrant with the scent of new forest growth.
Here, the creepers clinging to the whirlwinds, lightened by the absence of dust and petals cast off as they leap over the waters, hasten upward with great speed.
Here in these forest lands, the intervals between the circles of grass scattered by the wind appear white,
as if wild fires have entered them at will.
Here, the half-closed eyes of the deer are turbid from rolling in the mud.
In the evening, the herd of boars goes forth like a theater filled with water.
Here, in the forest villages, travelers drink the warm waters, which are indeed pale from the settling of milk-pails; (Gaüḍavaho 576–577).
Here, the wind—having pulled out the petals clinging to the roots honored by the water-lilies, and having startled the cranes—makes the lotus-stalks tremble. (Gaüḍavaha 578) [Āryā;

Here, something that has wandered about the sandy banks, fresh with the observation of flocks of birds descending from the branches of *taṃsī* trees, brings delight at evening; it is cool, becoming heavy with the falling of various creepers and flowers.
(Gauḍavaho 579) [Āryā] Saṅgalaṇa-māsalāanta-sīalō viviha-valli-kusumāṇa...
Even a single mango tree wanders here, fragrant with its exquisite and sweet scents.
(Gaüḍavaho 580) The leaves of the *āmalaka* trees, which hang down along this path, are uneven due to the pecking of parrots;
they are turned upward, greyish-brown, and edged with moss. (Gaüḍavaho 581)
Here, the forest lands—crowded with the sharp tools used for splitting *kakkola* fruits—are watched by travelers resting in the shade.
Here, the ground is stained yellowish-brown by the marks left by the cheek-salves of fair-skinned women separated from their lovers.
(Gauḍavaho 582) [Āryā] Here, the ground is stained yellowish-brown by the marks left by the cheek-salves of fair-skinned women separated from their lovers.
The fragrance of the *karahāṭa* flowers, sweet in the evening, wafts abroad.
The slightly cool scent of the *kalamba* flowers— whose filaments are pale-red and withered, and which are astringent from being steeped in the roots of fermenting liquor— is spreading.
Here, the fragrance of the *piyaṅgu* trees, tawny with the clusters of dates, wafts about, rendered astringent by the drops of nectar from the full-blown lotuses. (Gaüḍavaha 585) [Āryā;
Here, the fortune of the moonlight, cool with longing, rests upon the wild jasmine creepers that are naturally dense and pale-red at their tips, and upon the stars that are like *kunda* flowers.
The waves of the *java* flower clusters here have faded at the moment of being bitten by the bees.
The winds have cleared the boundaries where the pride of travelers was bewildered.
(Gauḍavaho 587) Here, the tips of the barley stalks, appearing like clusters of blossoms as they are thinned out by the ripening ears of grain, are being gathered at the borders. (Gauḍavaho 588)
Here, forest ponds, bright with rows of blooming *karavīra* flowers, are drunk by the eyes of the *tāpula*, *ulūpa*, *sugandha*, *java*, and *kaṣāya* trees.
Here, the earth is turned copper-red by the smoke of forest fires that has settled upon it. (Gauḍavaho 589) [Āryā]
Even during the day, the horizons appear as if stained by the darkness of night.
(Gaüḍavaha 590) Here, the traveler drinks in the entire interior of the orange fruit—reddish-grey and downy with its burst fibers—as if it were the lip of his beloved. (Gaüḍavaha 591)
In this cool season where flowers are sparse, Love here compels couples to engage in arm-wrestling, using a firm embrace as their weapon. (Gauḍavaha 592) [Āryā;
Here, the winds possess some indescribable splendor, having shaken off the forests and carrying the astringent fragrance of the filaments of the wandering *kāñcanāra* flowers.
Here, the *mādhavī* vines have as their ornament the slightly opened, tender sprouts bound together.
The bud, dark-red and stained by the throat of an old parrot, bursts open.
(Gaüḍavaho 594) Here, the forests have abandoned their nearby thickets of overgrown creepers;
they possess a variegated color, uneven and turbid, greenish-red and pale-yellow. (Gaüḍavaho 595)
How wonderful are these spring days, whose mouths are the mango blossoms— now green and now turning yellow as they are bound by fruit—
and whose throats possess unimpeded, sweet, and soft notes!
Surely it is out of curiosity for the new arrows that Cupid himself is manifesting himself here.
Even those who have never crossed the Sahāra river long for it here;

may there be prosperity for the village festival days, when children are filled with curiosity, women are heavy with pride in their new garments, and the villagers remain steadfast. (Gauḍavaho 597–598)

Here, upon the branches of the mango trees, clusters of blossoms are seen, speckled by bees perched at intervals, resembling the arrows of Love that have been only slightly consumed. (Gaüḍavaha 599) [Āryā;
Here, the forest regions, where the mango sprouts in their thickets are shining and the eyes of the deer are like lotuses, have attained awakening after sleeping soundly.
Here, the dark hue of the cheeks of the Śyāmala women from the Draviḍa country, who have been smeared with turmeric, [is visible]. (Gauḍavaho 600) [Āryā metre]

The fruit of the mango trees, depending on its transformation into an entire forest, brings delight. (Gaüḍavaha 601) [Āryā] Here, the dust from fresh wounds on the bamboo—charming with the powder of natural kaccūra, pale and crushed by the hooves of elephants—is rising up. (Gaüḍavaha 602) [Āryā]
Let not the flower-arrowed god of love become like Mādhava, whose bow is constantly drawn during the long winter nights and who has missed his mark;
for here, the tips of the sprouts emerge from the mouth of spring, glowing with a deep crimson. (Gauḍavaho 603) [Āryā meter]
Like young trees whose own sap has been extracted by the division of their branches, [the mango trees are seen];
here, somehow having obtained drops of the nectar of fresh *sahakāra* blossoms, they are being drunk by swarms of bees as they hum. (Gauḍavaho 604–605)
In this world, the fruit of mango trees—its bond weakened by the ripening of its stalk and stem—falls down in a sweet manner due to the weight of its juice. (Gauḍavaho 606) [Āryā;
These forest villages, delightful with their dwellings of wooden huts where children are delighted by the falling of fruit, captivate the heart;
even in these places, somewhat decayed by trees yet filled with smoke rising from the cowherds' stations, the heart is drawn. (Gauḍavaha 607) [Āryā metre]
[The traveler] lingers in villages where the crows perch sparsely upon tattered rags.

Here, he rests near a temple that has been swept clean by a pious villager who had come from the village; there is a deep, dark-blue pool, and a grove of massive trees fragrant with the scent of leaves. (Gauḍavaho 608–609)
In this place, where the roots of the *avamārua* trees are covered by budding sprouts,
the young birds on the summits of the peaks are merely making humming sounds; here,
the trees shine, resounding with the cries of many bees hovering about the branches.
The trunks of old trees are encircled by large clusters of bees;
here, the branches of the wood-apple trees, which first bent low with fruit, now yield only a faint hope for breath as their fruit is diminished by ripening and desiccation. (Gauḍavaho 611–612)
These young sprouts of the morning forest floor, their inner beauty marred by the dust of the feet of wayfarers, are fading away. (Gauḍavaho 613) [Āryā;
In the mountain ridges and caves, this water— tawny with the hue of withered bamboo leaves,
falling from the crumbling old boulders as it is turned green by moss— is trickling down. Here, in caves where the rocks have been worn away by the flow of water, sages dwell.
Bearing saffron robes as pale as old wood-apple seeds,
here on the slopes of the Niñcamālā mountains— whose cave-dwellings are occupied by perfected ones— the trees bear fruit for the bees who delight in their flowers. (Gauḍavaho 615–616)
Here the mountains have their surfaces made dusty by the heaps of powder remaining from the falling of massive, dragged-down rocks;
their rugged slopes are bright with minerals suitable for grinding into paste.
Here one may wander, where the diamond-hardness of the rocks is surpassed by the nails of those who dwell upon them.
Slowly, with the elephants, in the caves and temples of kuruvinda gems;
here, the rivers shine with their banks crumbling on this side, with few young fish, and with the foam providing the only semblance of water. (Gauḍavaho 618–619)
The mountain-village hamlets here abound in young Dhava thickets, beautiful with roots that cannot endure the peeling away of their bark;
they are like villages on mountain ridges where the liquor of intense passion is abundant. (Gaüḍavaho 620) [Āryā;
Even during this day, the edges of the mountain forests, soiled by the distant gaze and reddened by the sun as it turns behind the descent of the peaks, seem to smolder.
(Gauḍavaha 621) [Āryā meter] With their lower lips thin and curved, turned upward as they rest upon their feet...
The lion shines here while sleeping, its tips of claws protruding from its mane.
(Gauḍavaho 622) Here, the echo of the clanging sound of the struck bell-mouths is obstructed by a succession of wide-open mouths that have quickly become calm. (Gauḍavaho 623)
Here the sky appears, illuminated by the junctions of the masses of pure, shimmering jewel-stones,
and tawny with the tips of the petals of crushed pomegranate blossoms.
Here the peaks stand far away, while the broad slopes and manifest ridges lie close at hand.
The mountains appear at first dark at their peaks, gradually becoming bright at their bases.
Here, the grounds are thick with creepers clinging to the tops of trees stripped of their bark,
and uneven with the hollows and slopes of the roots of all the trees.
Here, the paths are marked by drops of blood, brilliant at their very tips, following the boars that have been struck by the arrows of the boar-hunters. (Gauḍavaho 627) [Āryā;
The pure ocean appears like the mass of the serpent Śeṣa’s hoods, its boundaries made manifest by the wealth spread out from the expanse of its jewels;
it is filled with clusters of date palms whose long trunks are entwined with thick leaves and stalks. (Gauḍavaho 628) [Āryā]
These forest groves along the shore of the ocean, dark as tamāla trees, bloom at dawn;
here, in the ponds, the lotus plants—like outposts of the Pallava tribes of the honey-bee Puliṃdas—are kissed by the beaks of swans. (Gauḍavaho 629–630)
Here, to the north of the ocean, on the mountain Udaya, the wind spreading through the sky follows Rāma and carries with it the fragrance of the forest creepers;
it is rendered pungent by the scent of the *pūtana* flowers rubbed against the pollen of the *pāṭalī*. (Gauḍavaho 631) [Āryā]
With his loincloth dyed by the *kavila* plant, the sun here appears like a lover to the people.
(Gaüḍavaha 632) In these mountain valleys, slippery with the spray of juice from palm trees split by the local winds and sweetly fragrant, the monkeys stumble and lick their hands. (Gaüḍavaha 633)
Here, the breeze causes the groves of *nālikera* trees to dance, their fruit-cases resonant with the mingling of the essence of ripened embryos within. (Gaüḍavaha 634) [Āryā;
The winds blow, carrying with them clusters of fruits from the *muhalandōlia* and *tāḍī* trees, which are entwined with tender sprouts and cause the royal grasses binding them to snap.
When Kailāsa moves, its shadow becomes dappled by the drops of frost. (Gauḍavaho 635) [Āryā]
The moon’s orb appears as if distressed by the grief of the destruction of its accumulated pride.

(Gaüḍavaha 636) Here, from his throat, which is constricted by the knot of the binding of Hara’s matted locks, the serpent Vāsuki releases gusts of wind borne upon his fully expanded hoods. (Gaüḍavaha 637)

Here, even during the nights, the branches of great medicinal herbs, entwined with the luster of jewels and with serpents crawling upon them due to their moisture, emerge from the waistbands [of the earth].
Here, at the jeweled peaks, the splendor of upturned peacock feathers is visible.
The scattering of rays, whose emergence is obstructed by veils of mist,
shines here with a pale hue— like clouds whose peaks have been shattered by the onset of the rains and which incessantly discharge streams of blood-red lightning. (Gauḍavaho 639–640)

Here, the beauty of the arms of the perfected beauties—which are like young leaves marked by fresh nail-wounds—surpasses the splendor of the king of creepers adorned with the rows of mango blossoms. (Gaüḍavaho 641) [Āryā] [p.

Here, the mountain caves—whose interiors are illuminated by the unwavering persistence of the ascetic vows of the best of sages—become, during their intervals of meditation, as it were, the dwellings of the Malaya mountains.
Here, the herds of buffaloes, looking about with faces turned toward the tips of the abandoned grass-blades, become [the objects of the gaze]. (Gauḍavaho 642) [Āryā metre]
The evenings of the day, in which the rays of the sun are hidden by the peaks of the mountains,

bring prosperity to those forest regions where the thickets are cooled by shadows, and where the paths at the edge of the woods are celebrated by the cowherd women returning from the city. (Gauḍavaho 643–644)
Here, the mountain ridges become lovely with groves being greyed by the rising smoke from the villages, and they grow deep with the onset of the arrival of the army columns.
Abandoning its evening luster, the sun emits rays as tawny as the tusks of an aged elephant.
Here shines the Lord of Night, his orb resting upon the peak of Mount Sumeru.
(Gaüḍavaho 646) Here, the rows of clouds, having settled upon the throats of aged kalaviṅka birds, resemble the sprouts of new kandalī plants drenched by showers of rain. (Gaüḍavaho 647)

Here, the fragrance of the filaments of the *taruṇa* trees, mingled with the water of the lake, wafts forth—sweet and intense, as if intoxicated by the wine of the ripened *kiṇva* flowers. (Gaüḍavaho 648) [Āryā;
In this first month of the rains, the forest deer drink the cool waters with their mouths only slightly opened, as if they were the very essence of the earth’s heat.
Here, the rivers are cool with the thick mud of the eggs of frogs that have burst open and been cast off by swaying trees.
The breezes blow, raising clouds of cool dust from the urine of the cattle.
(Gaüḍavaha 650) These wide-spreading floods flow along, their surfaces covered with bubbles that resemble scattered cow-dung, and variegated with the foam caught amidst the lush vegetation.
(Gaüḍavaha 651)
Here, the swarm of bees roams through the groves of *jambū* trees, where the astringent fragrance emanates from the fruit-stones washed by the falling rain;
here, the swarm roams through the thickets of *seriha* trees, whose filaments have been crushed.
The fragrance of the blooming *kalamba* flowers is cool upon the mountain ridges.
Here, during the rainy season, the excellence of the forest breezes—fragrant with the essence of mangoes and *mālūra* fruits drenched by the water—is fully manifested. (Gauḍavaho 653–654)
Here, the paths across the plains shine forth, made pure by dust settling from the nine streams, yet variegated by the grey scratches left by the hooves of deer. (Gaüḍavaha 655) [Āryā;
Even during the final watches of the night, the moonlight becomes dim; the breezes are gentle, and the nights are such that stars emerge from the sky as it is moist with water.
Here, she [is present], delightful with the nectar of the blossomed *sinduvāra* flowers... [Gauḍavaho 656, Āryā metre]...
of those [who are] bound by the joy of the Sinduvāra nectar.
The beauty of the autumn days blossoms upon the fragrant lotuses.

(Gaüḍavaha 657) Thus, by the soldiers of his army, who had traversed the entire circle of the earth bounded by all the quarters of the horizon, those forest regions were beheld as if they were the very abodes of happiness. (Gaüḍavaha 658)
Moreover—these regions of the mountain ridges have their shadows barely discernible due to the fading luster of the rainbow, which has lost its brilliance;
their splendor has been dispelled by the hooves of buffaloes. (Gaüḍavaho 659) [Āryā]
The shade of the trees in the groves, crushed by the branches of creepers that twist according to their will, is as harsh as the forest itself;
yet for those women whose gait is graceful, it is like another thing, with its filaments hidden within the breaking blossoms. (Gaüḍavaho 660) [Āryā]

Only the flowers of the creepers here wither away when pressed by their own fruit. (Gaüḍavaho 661) Those very same upper stories of the mansions, from which the connection of the roof-ridges has fallen away and where the surfaces of the walls have sagged in that manner, have now become mere ponds filled with clear water. (Gaüḍavaho 662)

Those very same processions have become such that their pillars are enriched by heaps of highly precious jewels, while their wealth consists merely of the gems on the hoods of the coiling serpents. (Gaüḍavaho 663) [Āryā metre]
Here is the city of Kirāta, surrounded by vast mounds of dust from its suburbs;
during the rainy seasons, its gems and coral are submerged in every corner and vicinity.
[Gaüḍavaha 664, Āryā meter] With its palaces, divine couches, and archways, its splendor emerges even more clearly as the dust settles.

Even though the city settlements are far away, they appear here as if nearby. (Gaüḍavaho 665) The dwellings of the houses here have openings scattered about for the search of wealth buried in the earth; their sites, where the grain-bins were once placed, are now rough with heaps of chaff and dust. (Gaüḍavaho 666)
Here, the fields have become thick with greenery as the furrows have grown deep with time;
they are dense thickets where mandāra trees flourish, spreading out through the excellence of the soil.
Tomorrow, when the earth is moist from the recent rains, they will appear as if rising up.

The gardens are like the quarters of the sky from which the fragrance of lotuses has been extracted. (Gaüḍavaha 668) In these groves, where the paths of the swings are strewn with sparse, withered darbha grass—its ropes broken by the weight of the branches—the young couples emerge. (Gaüḍavaha 669)

The borderlands here, where the red dust from the sites commemorating the fallen ancient kings has been stirred up by the aged serpents, are filled with the powder of decay. (Gaüḍavaho 670) [Āryā metre]
Here, in the ponds of lotuses and karavīras, the summer waters— having exhausted the essence of the kunda, uśīra, sahakāra, and pāṭala flowers— are becoming rare.
Here, along the edges, there are stone embankments with exposed roots, constructed from heaps of stones.
The undertakings of great men, though they have gone to ruin due to an uneven distribution,
remain even today like gateways whose tops are joined by pipes situated on difficult terrain and adorned with bells, appearing as if they still possessed abundant wealth. (Gauḍavaho 672–673)
The expanses of these mansions, with their wall-structures reaching up to the very peaks [of the towers], their wooden fastenings fallen away, and their inner courtyards now appearing desolate,
have doorways made of stones that are worn by the feet of people and devoid of the impurities of iron. (Gauḍavaho 674) [Āryā meter]
In this place, the entire forest of wood is consumed by a fire as light as a piece of agallochum;

these are the marshlands where the joints of the masses of reeds have been shattered, the long hanging tails have fallen off, and the broad phalluses of the crocodiles stand upright in the expanse of water. (Gaüḍavaho 675–676)
[102] Here, having seized a cluster of *ciñciṇī* fruits with his trunk,
the elephant devours the flower, which is as tawny as the feathers of an aged kalaviṅka bird. (Gaüḍavaha 677) [Āryā metre]
Here are seen dilapidated walls, once thickly plastered with reddish mud, now fallen away from their foundations and protruding from the broken edges of the masonry;
here they appear as circles of walls devoid of any coating of whitewash. (Gauḍavaho 678) [Āryā meter]
The wells and cisterns are overflowing with water that has risen to the brim;

Even today, O King, the streets here proclaim their depth by means of the jewel-studded thresholds, which are clearly visible as they crack slightly under the weight of their fullness. (Gauḍavaho 679–680)

In this time, the grounds— where the level courtyards and beautiful temples are seen only as slightly uneven due to their slight depressions and elevations— bear lines of powder clinging to the roots of doors that have been pulled down by the cattle of the householders. (Gauḍavaho 681) [Āryā meter]
The walls are crumbling, their plaster peeling away; the old walls are falling apart.

(Gaüḍavaho 682) Here, the birds in the cages seem to be entering deep into the interiors, while the houses, having only faintly obtained the shadow of pillars, appear as if they themselves have entered the shadows. (Gaüḍavaho 683)
Even by day, through the imagination of her presence, her limbs cause her to long for him; though silent here, they suddenly seem to be filled with sound. (Gaüḍavaho 684) [Āryā]
Here, the houses— devoid of fruit, leaves, iron, and copper, with their palm and date trees withered and their pillars crumbling from age like overturned iron—
appear as if they were the ruins of a king who was once recognized by his insignia but has now been seen only through the commencement of his destruction. (Gauḍavaho 685) [Āryā metre]

Even today, O Noble One, the paths to great treasures still exist in the surrounding regions. (Gaüḍavaha 686) Here, because smoke and dust do not rise, and because houses are sparse, the nights—once filled with the pleasures of love—become thick with darkness only after a long time. (Gaüḍavaha 687)
His own city was laid waste by enemy kings who had long been in his service but whose bonds of prosperity had been shattered; this was witnessed by them.
Furthermore, what happened—? *Gaüḍavaha* 688. [Āryā meter] What else occurred?

The face of this woman, its luster eclipsed as she gazes into a mirror, shines like a lotus kissed by the orb of the sun at dawn; it bears the reflection of the fading anger caused by her lover’s seizing of her lower lip. (Gauḍavaho 689) [Āryā]
Her speech is like wine whose intoxication flows from the mouth, and whose sweetness has burst forth;
her hand, with its fingers trembling as they rest upon the arm of her beloved who clings to her single breast that protrudes from her neck. (Gauḍavaho 690) [Āryā] [p. 104]
This face shines like the diversion of a lute made from a gourd-shell that has been hollowed out;
it bears a forehead adorned with a lock of hair held by her lover, like the orb of the first moon slowly emerging during the thick of night. (Gauḍavaho 691–692)
"Surely, for these two—the moon and the deer—who have been conquered by the radiance of her voice and eyes, a union has occurred as if they shared a common sorrow. (Gauḍavaho 693) [Āryā meter].
Thus, when he had lowered his bow during those playful activities of the rainy season...
His retinue describes the playful charms of the women of the army:
Moreover— of him,
from the temples of the enemy elephants, which were flowing with rut-ichor shaken by his blows...
The devotion of the bees is fixed upon flowers released from stalks. O King,
these women of that lord of Magadha do not appear radiant with smiles, as if pushed aside by the splendor of your abundant fame.

On their cheeks, which bear the likeness of the downy tufts of the fly-whisks used in their service, streaks of tears are seen as if they were streams of tears born of inner fear. (Gauḍavaho 697) [Āryā;
O King, from the hollows of the temples of those elephants of yours—

those conquerors of the hosts of enemies— the darkness, as it were, issues forth, driven out by the rays of the pearls situated in their frontal globes, through the friction of the dust, mothers-of-pearl, and lotus-fibers. (Gauḍavaho 698) [Āryā]

They merely pass their time by throwing themselves against the mountain ridges; or else, under the guise of smoke emitted from their hard bones struck by the edges of their chisels, they vomit it forth. (Gauḍavaha 699) [Āryā]
The mass of rays, like a veil of darkness consumed by the splendor of that day, spreads forth;
fragments of the day are fashioned according to the measure of the passing moments, while heaps of entire bodies are cast up as if by the stroke of a chisel. (Gauḍavaho 700–701)
His face appears like the orb of the moon, encircled by the radiance of his pure teeth shining forth from his smile, as if it were the moonlight clinging to it upon entering the sky.
(Gaüḍavaho 702) [Āryā meter] His limbs, severed by the blows of weapons and hacked by the strokes of axes, fall apart.
Standing firm in battle against the Asuras who had bestowed happiness upon them, their weapons were shattered. Thus,
that Sun-god as well— his orb made doubly brilliant by the mending of those very weapons—
does not fill the quarters, his rays flickering due to your majesty.
Even by others, their foreheads bowed low as they avoid your crest-jewels from afar, a prostration is performed as if with the knitting of frowns upon their upturned brows. (Gaüḍavaha 705) [Āryā]
It is true that when you are seen, it does not appear as though there are others like you;
rather, your very sight establishes the majesty of Time alone. When you are remembered by your lord, the cruelty of Fate does not cause him pain.
Even though the rainy season is near, the summer causes the forest groves to sprout new shoots. (Gaüḍavaho 707) How can those whose virtues are innate be called devoid of virtue?
Even they who are without virtue rejoice as if they were virtuous by relying upon you. (Gaüḍavaho 708)
With his right arm supported by you, who are like the goddess Śrī herself, this hand of his incessantly releases a rain of gold.
Having a thousand mouths at his disposal, why indeed would Vāsuki not praise him? (Gauḍavaho 709) [Āryā meter]
If one is able to contemplate even a single virtue with a focused heart, then those marks drawn by the Creator upon the foreheads of men— which result in such strange consequences—
touch them, O Lord of the Earth, under the guise of their prostrating at your feet. (Gauḍavaho 710–711)
In the act of drawing [his sword], that reflection of the enemy’s glory formed upon the unsheathed blade appears upon you,
O Sahasāhava, as if you were suddenly clothed in blue garments. (Gaüḍavaha 712) [Āryā]

Even though the common letters of your name were established in the science of grammar, you throb only within the heart by virtue of being merely recited; O sword, your [fame] arises from the state of being pearls on the tusks of elephants struck down by your edge. (Gauḍavaho 713) [Āryā meter]
It mimics the play of a torrential downpour of rain; [so does your fame].
(Gauḍavaho 714) Your attendants perceive it as "passionate love," while your enemies perceive it as the "glow of the fire of anger";
thus, they find vermilion in the seals of your commands. (Gauḍavaho 715)
How indeed could Fortune, whose abode is the left arm, dwell upon your sword?
It is understood that her reflection is seen here because she is stationed upon it. Even so, the virtues of the world do not become manifest through their own excellence.
O Lord, they depart having been weighed down by your honor, yet they attain renown.
(Gaüḍavaho 717) Indeed, you have not even from the very beginning been made an object of mockery by enemies who have bound their crests with their feet;
rather, they undergo the exertion of knitting their brows as if out of fear of some offense committed against you. (Gaüḍavaho 718)

O Lord, by the unceasing streams of tears from the co-wives of your rivals, the dangling creepers of their long tresses appear as if they have been uprooted along with their roots. (Gauḍavaho 719) [Āryā]
Knowing that there is no human agency in them, how could the Goddess Śrī abide in those who are like young women?
How indeed can women desire men, when these women are themselves such?
Some have perished by the sword, while others have sought refuge in the forest alone.
It is said that the remaining enemies have also disappeared somewhere into the ocean.
(Gaüḍavaho 721) Like seeds on the earth, men arise from various lineages; they descend, ascend, and move about like roots and sprouts. (Gaüḍavaho 722)
O King, you alone have bestowed upon her the reputation for fickleness that belongs to Fortune;
she, in turn, has granted you sovereignty free from the faults of a master.
Yet, O Lord of Men, this appears to you as if it were the very opposite, even though it is the essence of discernment.
You are afraid of faults, yet they have perished because of you.

O King, throughout all the quarters of the world, your stainless virtues are seen following after you like washermen following behind the elephants of the directions with their cool waters. (Gauḍavaho 724–725)
The world-honored ones are captivated by your virtues, yet you, O good man, are captivated even by a mere fraction of their virtues; thus, you are superior to the virtuous. (Gaüḍavaho 726) [Āryā]

O Lord, those seeds of wealth which were watered by the rain of your gifts and sown in the fields of the earth have now, in due time, grown into fruition for you. (Gaüḍavaho 727) [Āryā meter] Having transferred [your favor] to suppliants whose pride was swollen by the attainment of their great desires...
I think that even with such sovereignty, pride does not manifest within you. O King,
having received [wealth] from you and giving it away here and there,
other kings have caused your tree of charity to grow far, as if by means of branches.

The necklaces of pearls are beautiful, providing pleasure as they are formed by the holes made by the sharp javelins thrust into the temples of your enemy elephants; and furthermore— (Gaüḍavaha 730) [Āryā]
Her hand, with its webbed membrane slackened and hanging loose, rests upon the place of the hard, firm pillow of her swelling breasts;
her bangles on the lotus-like hands, whose fingers are trembling, are slipping off from the loosened webs. (Gauḍavaho 731) [Āryā metre]

With their limbs seen broken and slightly slackened, they appear as if their bellies have been split open; marked by rows of teeth protruding painfully from the tightly closed door, they receive [their fate].
(Gaüḍavaha 732) [Āryā] [p. 110] gāḍha-kavāḍaa-dukkhuccuḍanta-ṇaharāi-lañchaṇō lahaï.
The expanse of her breasts possesses the beauty of the lunar orb emerging from the clouds;
the mass of her hair, like a cluster of disheveled and swaying creepers, perfumes the region of her nostrils with breaths that expand as they are released from her throat. (Gaudavaho 733–734)

The pair of her arms shines, their breasts restrained by modesty, while the distress of her hands arises from the loosening of her jeweled bracelets; thus, O Lord, having removed her bodice during the heat of the day due to her heavy burden, she performs her ablutions at dusk. (Gauḍavaho 735) [Āryā meter]
The army, accompanied by women whose husbands were dear to them and who were dressed in charming attire, ascended your bedchamber;
thus, that host which had previously been the terror of the city of Jayantī, now became one whose activities were occupied solely with amorous play. (Gaüḍavaho 736–737)
Moreover— the face, its luster copper-red with indignation caused by the suspicion of a mental agitation, becomes as if closed in meditation, yet with its lips quivering. (Gaüḍavaho 738) [Āryā]

Her gaze opens wide, fierce with the corners of her eyes reddened by a slight, lingering anger; it possesses the luster of the jeweled frontal globes of a rutting elephant-king whose ears are flapping. (Gaüḍavaha 739) [Āryā] [p.

The moon, having relinquished its earthly beauty because it was surpassed by the brilliance of her face, suffers a loss of its fullness and the luster of its throat; yet, when struck by the mass of flames from the submarine fire at the edge of the netherworld, its surface cracks apart. (Gauḍavaho 740) [Āryā]
In some way or another, her eye was contracted by the dense knitting of her eyebrows.

(Gaüḍavaho 741) Thus, although his body has been consumed by the fire of the Three-Eyed One’s wrath, the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma), having sat down before Jānuvī, remains today as the very embodiment of perverse arrows in the world. (Gaüḍavaho 742)

The tresses of their hair were disheveled, their pair of eyes rolled about like stars, their ornaments were in disarray, and their faces had eyes trembling with amorous play; the girth of the necks of those women was embraced by the thick, lotus-stalk-like arms of their lovers. (Gaüḍavaha 743) [Āryā]
That dandy displays the splendor of his own jewelry;
by him, the fresh flower of the *kalamba*—fragrant with its filaments—is led to the state of a crest-jewel, surpassing even the young sprouts. (Gauḍavaho 744–745)

The cool breezes at the beginning of the night, fragrant with the scent of ketaka flowers from the groves that have opened their petals in the pleasant season, steal away his heart. (Gaüḍavaho 746) [Āryā] [p.
The nights, their moons fragmented by clouds dense with the sweet fragrance of blooming water-lilies, grow dear to him whose tears have not yet ceased;
the fragrant sighs of the women flash forth at every moment of separation from him. (Gauḍavaho 747) [Āryā meter]
He appears like a fragment of the elephant of Love, with flower-arrows fixed in his heart;
he is seen by their eyes, which run toward both directions with tears of joy,
as if those eyes were the blossoming lotuses of their embrace.

Moreover— those whose lines of body hair suddenly resemble waves of wrinkles, appearing like the tips of braided locks on their backs visible through the gaps between their ribs. (Gauḍavaho 750) [Āryā]
With smiles that follow the luster of their lips, they cause the moon to appear as if newly risen, its deer-mark obscured by the moisture of their sighs;

Those girls, whose childhood has reached its final stage, display their budding breasts, which possess the playful charm of lovely creepers;
they suddenly appear as if covered by a dark blue garment, like a swarm of bees, with their flower-like teeth slightly protruding. (Gauḍavaho 752–753)

May those who, having bestowed the intoxication of passion with their very glance, drink from the bodies of others the red *asoka* juice— the essence of fresh sprouts of nails— [grant you prosperity]. (Gaüḍavaho 754) [Āryā]
In the presence of their lovely green garments, which have been seized by chance, the thighs display their state of being like the interior of plantain trees, possessing a peerless retinue;
while upon the surface of their breasts, the playfully lowered faces act as a pair of ointment-pots, with the fragments of their lips serving as the pigment. (Gauḍavaho 755) [Āryā]
Know that their hearts throb like wounds from the manifest arrows of Love.

(Gaüḍavaho 756) By whom the three-eyed Śiva’s eye was captivated as if it were looking upward at the wound of the bodiless God of Love between the breasts, where the pearl necklace serves as the pupil.
(Gaüḍavaho 757)
The line of hair on her breasts, its placement slightly broken by horripilation,

resembles a trail of hoof-marks left by the chariot of Love as it hastens toward her beloved, fearing a moment’s separation. (Gauḍavaho 758) [Āryā] Just like the wheel-track of the chariot of Love traveling toward the beloved.
They shine with their orb-like breasts, broadened by the acquisition of embraces;
they see their feet being abandoned for the service of *campaka* buds, as if seized out of fear of blows from the lotuses of their ears, by the garlands of lamps. (Gauḍavaho 759–760)

With their eyelashes slightly contracted due to the influence of a mixture of bashfulness and the sight [of him], they hold their beloved as if cherished, fearing that he might depart. (Gaüḍavaho 761) [Āryā metre]
They shine with blood-red rays from their teeth, which are slightly crimson from the taste of food;
these rays, spreading across her breasts, appear like the arrow-wounds of the God of Love.
(Gaüḍavaho 762) [Āryā meter] By virtue of their length and breadth, they are fit only for a firm embrace by the hands.
They forcibly place flower garlands upon those who have no desire for their husbands.
(Gaüḍavaho 763) Even while their lovers are away, they bathe the statues of those beloved ones with tears when they are defiled by intimacy with other women. (Gaüḍavaho 764)
