At the appointed time, with their eyes blooming as they gaze upon the faces of their beloveds, they loosen their golden girdles, which are brilliantly radiant from the friction of their contact;
their breasts are filled with the pollen-dust from the ear-flowers trembling at the touch of their paramours. (Gauḍavaha 765) [Āryā]
They sprinkle, as it were, the wounds of Love that have barely healed and remain fixed;

trembling flows forth from their breasts, where the necklaces jingle against hands placed thereon, while the girdles and anklets on their limbs have become silent as they are held fast. (Gauḍavaho 766–767)

Those women who, as if with various upper garments of lotus filaments pierced by the earring-jewels of their hearts, seem to paint their lovers with eyes bristling with the downy fibers of their colored lashes. (Gaüḍavaha 768) [Āryā meter]
Whose stainless fringes are reflected in every direction, whose toes are soft as if massaged by the goddess Śrī herself,
and whose lotuses are shimmering with tremulous playfulness directed toward their beloved— [those women are like the quarters of the sky]. (Gauḍavaho 769) [Āryā metre]
Their eyes, with their lashes like wings, flutter upward;

as they drink the nectar of the mouth with playful lotus-stalks, they do so through the presence of the rays of teeth clearly manifesting as they touch the lips of their beloved nearby. (Gauḍavaho 770–771)
In those young women, their graceful charms shine as if they were being bound by his virtues, while their hearts tremble, being carried away by the new passion for him.
Upon his chest, the circle of Śyāmā’s breasts quivered from the pressure of her embrace. (Gauḍavaho 772) [Āryā metre]
She attains the shade of a lotus leaf placed playfully upon her lap.
(Gaüḍavaha 773) Other young women desire nothing but his beauty, being indifferent to all other virtues.
Or who else would seek a flower fragrant as the petals of the *indīvara*? (Gaüḍavaha 774)
The gaze of playful women rests for a moment upon the orb of their hips, where the silken garment is pressed tight by the girdle pulled down by their left hands. (Gaüḍavaho 775) [Āryā]
Her smile is pure, her face is like a blooming *nava-vaula* flower white as the cheeks, and her waist,
freed from its girdle, is the very life of graceful charms. (Gauḍavaho 776) [Āryā] And furthermore—
Upon her head—where the shoulders are reached by a fresh braid adorned with tiny earrings—a beautiful floral crest-jewel shines, set with a lovely top-knot gem.
It steals away the heart, with saffron applied to the edges of her lips that have been rubbed away. (Gauḍavaho 777) [Āryā]
Her lotus-face has its dark, slightly upturned eyebrows drawn across the sky;
it possesses a fresh unguent applied to the path of her curved eye-corners, which extends like a streak of rut-fluid from her intoxicated navel down to the surface of her cheeks. (Gauḍavaho 778–779)
The surface of her breast, its expanse shimmering with the luster of a necklace of gems within,
is made beautiful by an ornament of variegated flower-clusters scattered upon it. (Gauḍavaho 780) [Āryā meter] Thus,
the fragrance of betel-leaf infused with slightly visible wine captivates the heart.
The *piyā-sattha* (the treatise on the beloved) consists of subtle cleansing, ornaments, supports, and ointments.
Furthermore, what has been produced? [Gaüḍavaho 781; Āryā meter; p. 117]
The gaze of young women rests upon the moon-like faces of their lovers, which are as white as lotus-ponds and possess the luster of teeth;
yet, within those faces—where passion is firmly established by the suppression of their natural bashfulness—their love begins to blossom forth.
(Gaüḍavaho 782) [Āryā meter] It breaks out from the state of being hidden by the firm onset of passion.
In the season of spring, the royal splendor resides in the rows of fresh *bakula* trees;
first, the enthusiasm for adornment spreads through the festive preparations, as the night-garlands are taken up, pale with frost. (Gauḍavaho 783–784)

Upon her face, which is jagged with the remains of a garland of jasmine buds, there flashes the glow of saffron— tender as the first touch of the moon— as the petals of the damanaka flowers fall away,
variegated by their contact with the parched desert wind. (Gauḍavaho 785) [Āryā metre]

In the winter, when the moon has assumed the guise of a yellow *piyaṅgu* flower rising at the breaking of night, that host of beloved women has abandoned their charming ornaments, their tresses being smeared with saffron and white *kunda* flowers.

(Gaüḍavaha 786) In the winter, when the moon has assumed the guise of a yellow *piyaṅgu* flower rising at the breaking of night, that host of beloved women has abandoned their charming ornaments, their tresses being smeared with saffron and white *kunda* flowers. (Gaüḍavaha 787)
Moreover— the wind makes the mango blossoms rustle with a soft *jhana* sound, their heads loosened and clinging as they are pushed down by the emergence of fruit. (Gauḍavaha 788) [Āryā]
The fragrance of the *sattala* flowers,
whose stalks are rooted in the hearts of women and whose waters are infused with the essence of their sighs, spreads through the night. (Gaüḍavaha 789) [Āryā]

In these days, which are pleasant with the ripening of the glory of spring, the dwellings of the groves— where the mādhavī creepers stand solitary and lusterless with their single flowers, where the clusters of blossoms possess stainless fragrance, and where they are thick with knots of fruit— [are being visited by her]. (Gauḍavaho 790) [Āryā metre]
They rejoice amidst the throngs of female attendants in the city enclosures.
Moreover—[their] cheeks are radiant with the edges of fresh, tender dates that have been chewed to the core. (Gauḍavaho 791) [Āryā] And furthermore—
The loveliness of their eyes shines forth, as the collyrium has melted away from the corners of their gaze.
(Gaüḍavaho 792) Their eyes, with their white brilliance slightly dimmed by the faint closing of their lids, come like new moons with shimmering stars.
(Gaüḍavaho 793)

With his chin slightly lowered due to the thinness of his cheeks, and his bright lower lip intent upon the chewing of betel-rolls, he appears like a young elephant with its temples thin from the flow of ichor, its face pale, and its bright lower lip intent on the chewing of young *kesara* filaments reddened by heat.
(Gauḍavaho 794) [Āryā] Of those [filaments] which are pale from tenderness and possess the quality of fresh *kesara* blossoms reddened by heat...
Like the slight virility found in the breasts of young girls, so it was with those whose innocent nature was bound by the first onset of love for him.
(Gaüḍavaho 795) [Āryā meter, p.
119] Thus, among those whose simple hearts were attached to the pursuit of their first passion for him...
His gaze rested upon young women whose amorous gestures were languid with modesty.

(Gaüḍavaho 796) Then, for him who had fixed the entire burden of the world upon the pillars of his firm arms, Bappairāja was but a mere trifle, like fuel for the fire of the monkey-king (Rāma). (Gaüḍavaho 797)
Even though it is but a mere fragment, it appears full of flavor;
for it has somehow been grasped with great respect by the feet of Śrī Kamalāyudha.
Like drops of the nectar of the wine of poetry emerging from the ocean that is Bhavabhūti, they sparkle. (Gauḍavaho 798) [Āryā]
He whose distinctive excellences are still manifest in the compositions of narratives;
he who found joy in the speech of Jalamitra, in Kuntideva, in Raghava, in Subandhu, and in Bandhuvarman. (Gaudavaho 799–800)
It is painted, full of flavor, thoroughly seasoned, substantial,
stable, radiant, dense with shadow, and embellished with song. (Gaüḍavaho 801) [Āryā meter] Those who know the meters are experts in the speech of the Āgamas, such as Bharata, Gōama, and others.

Thus do they rejoice in him who causes laughter, who is a poet of essence, and who—desiring to be perfumed by the many virtues of poets—abides in the ears of the learned. (Gaüḍavaha 802) [Āryā; p. 120]
"Excellent! Well spoken! they cried, their heads nodding in wonder.
Then, as the assembly sat together, he was addressed by the learned men during the course of a conversation among virtuous souls, their eyes wide with amazement.
The serpent-king bears upon his shoulders, which are as beautiful as the earth girded by the mass of clouds, a circle of hoods that remains somehow expanded even when contracted;
they appear like the staffs of smoke from clouds swelling at the time of the world’s destruction. (Gauḍavaho 805) [Āryā]
With the pillars of their trunks raised for a moment as the elephants of the quarters plunge into the water,
and with the solar disc revolving within the circles of their flickering trunks,
the oceans become like the submarine fire upon the path of the sky.

The masses of clouds, with their circles of flickering lightning, settle down like those who have drunk the water on that day, as if out of compassion for the ocean, whose waters were exhausted by Murāri as he reclined upon his bed within his watery abode.
(Gauḍavaho 808) [Āryā] By the ocean... of Murāri, who was reclining upon his bed embraced by the water-abode.
The sun, enveloped by the *vīti* plant, is given as if it were a great lamp;
other colors and tastes arise, becoming quite different for those who are mingled together. (Gaüḍavaho 809) [Āryā] [p. 121]
Meru,

its peaks ascended by the throngs of gods clamoring as they emerge, and resounding with the tumultuous roar of waters as they overflow from the caverns, bathes all the oceans which have been rendered turbid by the agitation caused by the churning of the Mandara mountain. (Gauḍavaho 810–811)
In a world filled with the waters of the deluge due to the agitation caused by falling at his feet,
the Three-Eyed Lord ascends, as it were, a royal boat in the form of the crescent moon upon his crest.
(Gauḍavaho 812) [Āryā] For one whose expansion of breath is restrained by the persistence of youth, there is a state of agitation.
Even for the Self-born One (Brahmā), whose face was submerged in the waters of the ocean;

and when the gods were distressed by the mountain of the gods (Mount Mandara) shaking as it was tossed by the waters of the dissolution—Murārī (Viṣṇu) became the support for the three worlds, remaining unharmed. (Gauḍavaho 813–814)

He whose great column of smoke is seen by the sun— with its rays acting as petals joined at the tip— as if it were a palmyra tree bearing the fruit of a unique poet; of him indeed this [work] is heard, which has assumed the title *Vigrahatunga*.
Or rather, he is the outflow of the essence of the enemy of the great Asura lineage of the world. (Gaüḍavaha 816) [Āryā] [p.
122] Or else:

The mass of clouds, tossed by the pressure of the limbs clashing in their haste, with all its web of lightning-bolts momentarily shattered, retreats; released from the breaking clouds and deceived by the turning celestial chariots, it somehow... [Gaüḍavaho 817] (Āryā metre)
The flashes of lightning, their beauty of plumage lost as they fall,
descend like great birds whose wings have become stones, having wandered through the sky in association with the clouds of dust rising from the ocean of the battle. (Gauḍavaho 818–819)
The path of gold appears, yellowed by the luster of the jewels at the base of the ocean revealed by the submarine fire, like a road first reddened and then pushed forward by the dawn.
Spreading forth, it resembles the flame of the submarine fire rising from the depths of the ocean, doubled by the brilliance of the gods' weapons.
The lords of serpents, whose hoods were shattered by their wives and who rolled about with faces distorted, fled like Garuḍas.
(Gaüḍavaho 821) Ananta endures the world encircled by the motionless hoods held steady at the base, while his other hoods remain joined to Garuḍa. (Gaüḍavaho 822)

Even the showers from the clouds disperse; for the thunderbolts, though as hard as the vajra of the Lord of Birds, shatter against his chest, which is calloused by the scars of being struck by Mount Mandara. (Gauḍavaho 823) [Āryā] [p.

The serpents, due to their contact with the Lord of Birds who was falling as he was driven away by their own taxes, suffer with a fury doubled by the sight of their helpless faces. (Gauḍavaho 824) [Āryā meter] With the trunk of his hand made resonant by the sighs stirred up by the elephants of the quarters moving in agitation...
Like the name of the remaining race of serpents, it sinks down into the underworld.
Thus, this [king], whose fierce fame is esteemed by the multitude of venomous snakes, bubbles up with humility toward the state of Kṛṣṇa through his modesty. (Gauḍavaho 825–826)

Moreover— the expanse of the sky flashes forth, as if fierce with the staff-like tresses of women standing with their hair disheveled by the heat, mingled with the filaments of the masses of Vidyādharas wandering in confusion. (Gaüḍavaha 827) [Āryā]
The moon bears a cluster of stars fashioned like a bimba fruit,
appearing like the jagged remnants of fangs shattered and left behind during the merciless devouring of the mountain peak.
[Gaüḍavaho 828] The shadow of the anklets cast by the Fortune of the Three Worlds as she trembles, shaken by his wrath...

The solar disc, pierced by the boar’s tusk, shatters in the sky. (Gaüḍavaho 829) [Āryā] The solar disc appears like a young gourd-pot, its interior liquefied by sudden bursting, with the mud of its pulp scattered by the rays as if it were a pool of liquid. (Gaüḍavaho 830) [Āryā]

The victorious horses neigh as if divided by the dark luster of iron bits placed in their mouths at the beginning of that day, while they are soiled by the smoke from the chariots they have swiftly borne. (Gaüḍavaha 831) [Āryā metre]
At that moment, when his body became bent by the contraction of his eyebrows that emerged instantly, terrible portents arose throughout the worlds. Moreover—: *Gauḍavaho* 832 [Āryā] Furthermore—:

The flower-garland, its ends heavy with clusters of clinging *priyaṅgu* blossoms, glitters as it swings; it delights the heart, shimmering upon the thighs that ripple with the movement of her girdle, and bound by the string of her waistband like a pair of earrings. (Gauḍavaha 833) [Āryā metre]
The mass of her hair, loosened by the exertion of dancing in an irregular manner,
bears a decoration of damanaka flowers that is jagged with lovely mādhavī blossoms and possesses a dusty-yellowish hue from the pollen clinging to her breasts. (Gauḍavaho 834–835)
Her gaze—slightly heavy with lashes grey with the dust of her couch, languid from the fading effects of wine, and casting wide, sparse glances—rolls about;
thus, this one who revels in the thick essence of play blooming at the festival of love brings delight. (Gauḍavaha 836) [Āryā meter]
In the pleasure-houses of this [king], there is a multitude of new amorous delights. (Gaüḍavaho 837) [Āryā meter] [p.
125] And furthermore—
Even the completed virtues of one whose expansion has been obstructed by the suspicion that their objects are insignificant appear as if they were never completed for long.
(Gaüḍavaho 838) Or rather:

Her face—its cheeks flushed by the enjoyment of abundant pollen from the flowers of the *vasuhā* tree—is being kissed by the women as it becomes pale like the winter moon; her forehead is adorned with fine hair-tips emerging from their roots in a manner beyond compare. (Gauḍavaho 839) [Āryā]
With their eyes, which were weary from resting upon sighs emitted from their palates,
casting glances that were lovely with fresh tears of joy— glances whose outer corners were made languid by hanging drops of tear-drops as large as mustard seeds; (Gaüḍavaho 840–841)

Bearing a slightly reddened palm with its thumb-tip pressed down and its sprout-like fingers extended in a gesture of apprehension, she utters a sweet cry to the gods, while her heart—fashioned by Love itself—trembles for a moment from the pangs of pain.
(Gauḍavaho 842) [Āryā meter] Thus, this [woman], whose heart is fashioned by Love... through momentary faltering sensations...
The captive bards of the rival king are seen with their faces turned toward the ground in secret.
Just as the Lord of Magadha was previously brought to ruin by this exalted one,
so do these [bards], desiring everything from you, wish for him to be beheaded.
[126] Having laughed softly, he spoke with overflowing sincerity: "The hearts of the pure are indeed indifferent to any sense of obligation. (Gaüḍavaha 845) [Āryā]
How could the grief and agitation stored in the hearts of the steadfast ever vanish?
Yet, joy, however slight, makes even the limbs of the great tremble. (Gaüḍavaho 846) [Āryā] It rolls repeatedly in her throat, faltering and agitated by joy.
The winds seem to issue forth from my mouth in praise of my lord.
(Gauḍavaho 847) [Āryā meter] And furthermore: He bears aloft his expanded hood-circle like an inner garment.
The serpent Śeṣa, with his long body trailing behind him due to the deceptive movement of his tail, [assumes this form].
(Gaüḍavaho 848) With four humps formed by his feet whose luster rivals the moon, and with his head hidden, he truly attains the shape of a tortoise. (Gaüḍavaho 849)

With his snout raised and stirred up by the first rising and tossing, and with his broad forehead marked by the ichor flowing from his high, moist temples, he emerges, emitting a series of "hum" sounds caused by the pain of his body's twisting movements. (Gauḍavaho 850) [Āryā metre]
The smoke ends where the dense darkness of the netherworld begins. [Gaüḍavaho 851] [Āryā meter] [p.
127] In the path beneath the netherworld, [it flows] broken, scattered, slackened, and fallen.
The essence of the fresh sprouts of the *rocanā* plant is extracted by means of Mount Sumeru.
(Gauḍavaho 852) Due to its nature of changing in an instant, the appearance of the teeth becomes jagged with grass playfully chewed, like the tips of sprouts slightly emerged. (Gauḍavaho 853)
By the weight of the streams of thick, spreading milk flowing at that very moment, Śeṣa appears like a mountain at its base, burdened by the weight of supporting the earth.
Thus, by him, she was made to tremble with the agitation of her sudden onset of cow-like behavior. (Gauḍavaho 854) [Āryā]
By him, whose own name was marked by the title "Lord of the Earth upon Earth" (Puhaī-puhaī-vaïṇā)—even he cannot endure a comparison with this [work].
To whom indeed do the flashes of glory belonging to the rest of those deceived by false pride not seem bitter? (Gauḍavaho 855–856)
Moreover:

Know that even wealth equal to an ornament brings defilement; even as it increases, it causes the moon to lose its luster, just as a shower of frost does, even though it is concordant with it. (Gauḍavaho 857) [Āryā]
Likewise, masters are so provoked by sycophants with their praises of delusion that they think nothing at all even when excellent qualities have been manifested. (Gaüḍavaho 858) [Āryā;

For indeed, O King, the path for those who possess the nourishment of virtues is easy to find; but for others, who are destitute of virtue, the path must be sought everywhere. This, truly, is the secret of Fortune: that even one whose heart is solely intent on seeking the path of good conduct [is not easily found].* *Note: The final line appears to contain a wordplay or paradox regarding the rarity of such a person despite their pursuit of virtue.*

The world does not perceive one who surrenders oneself through virtues. (Gaüḍavaho 860) Discernment does not tolerate a fault that is rooted in good character; rather, it merely waits for the master to attend to the fault when it is disguised as a virtue. (Gaüḍavaho 861)
Even a conduct that is not grasped by the world, though established in prosperity and serene, yet having reached desolation,
is like a flower that has fallen upon the very tip of its fruit. (Gaüḍavaha 862) [Āryā meter] Even for one who is constantly anxious about guarding wealth, wife, and secrets, there is misfortune.
Even so, O lords of men, there are those who possess groups of near relatives.
(Gaüḍavaho 863) [Āryā] Behold this reversal: much wine makes one intoxicated, yet very little wealth does not;
whereas very little wealth makes one intoxicated, much wine does not do so. (Gaüḍavaho 864) [Āryā]
Even those who have manifested excellent qualities and attained prosperity become devoid of qualities;
yet those who have attained fortune while remaining entirely without qualities are far indeed from true virtues. (Gauḍavaho 865) [Āryā] [p.
Some, being of a fickle nature, attain great wealth and prosperity through their virtues;
others, though pure in conduct, seek virtues by means of their riches. Houses filled with wicked attendants and treacherous masters are avoided.
In that very same way, they gradually came to consider even the wicked as virtuous.
(Gaüḍavaho 867) Indeed, by this much alone do those devoid of discrimination adopt virtues; yet by this much alone do masters become averse to the great. (Gaüḍavaho 868)

Thus, through their virtues, they have become such that even their entire ocean of faults is no longer a cause for pride among all good people; yet now, O King, those very faults, when perceived as virtues, clearly bear fruit. (Gauḍavaho 869) [Āryā]
Even faults become virtues through the estimation of excellence;
when people are deluded, what else do noble men resort to but the concealment of their true nature, distressed by the failure of others to discern the essence of their qualities? (Gaüḍavaha 870–871)
Day by day, they are tormented by two kinds of sufferings:
those that arise during the time of good men, and whatever arises during the time of base men. (Gaüḍavaho 872) [Āryā] [p.

Those who grant an audience and the favor of their presence to those of noble mind and virtuous conduct consider that to be the fruit of the loom, for it is the very fruit of their own [meritorious] deeds.
(Gaüḍavaho 873) [Āryā meter] Even another person indeed enjoys the pleasures of wealth as if they were effortless and natural.
Only in the act of doing what is improper does the master’s majesty overflow;
when a wrong has been committed against great men who are at their end, the heart finds relief only upon seeing the wicked man’s high regard for the master. (Gauḍavaho 874–875)

Even if there are some virtuous men in the palaces of kings who seem to share the common lot of ordinary people, that is due to some other cause entirely; for it is by those very same qualities that good men are reduced to the status of courtesans in the presence of kings. (Gauḍavaho 876)
Who indeed would not seek out those very virtues with great respect? (Gaüḍavaho 877) [Āryā] Who would not turn their face away from the virtueless? Whom do the virtuous not distress?
Who is not virtuous? And who is not devoid of virtue? Only he lives happily. (Gaüḍavaho 878) [Āryā]
That the heart of masters, exhausted by its service toward kinsmen, now turns away from them—this is indeed due to the fear of losing this jewel-ornament out of pride. (Gauḍavaho 879) [Āryā;
Those who lack discernment and are devoid of virtue praise the virtues of others;
however, masters who have themselves acquired such virtues are exceedingly hostile toward the virtues of others.
Indeed, everyone, being eager for the excellence of their own virtues, harbors the arrogance of envy.

Those who cannot endure the excellence of another's virtues are base and devoid of merit. By means of even a little good conduct, one is perceived as a true friend by others; indeed, it is for oneself alone that one must strive through hardship in this world.

How indeed can even those established in humility grasp the mere garland of virtues, when that very same garland, once abandoned, shines with double its former brilliance when it is embraced? (Gauḍavaho 883) [Āryā] If, being tormented in their hearts, they think something— well, I do not know.

Furthermore, virtuous people do not become offended even when their actions are directed toward them. (Gaüḍavaho 884) Virtues bestow honor upon faults, and even faults bestow honor upon a treasury of virtues;
if those faults which are themselves virtues belong to virtues, then homage to them! (Gaüḍavaho 885)
Even the wicked appear as friends, and even friends display the behavior of the wicked;
this alone is the boundary between virtues that shine afar. (Gaüḍavaho 886) [Āryā] [p.
Having cultivated faults, one is able to establish oneself in virtues;
once one has emerged into virtues, the mind no longer settles upon faults.
Even if his virtues are utterly diminished, a good man remains equal to others.
Even when their essence has vanished, the benefit to the world remains intact in those who possess self-restraint. (Gaüḍavaha 888) For women, quarrels and intoxication are their mirrors;
for men, however, conduct alone is the mirror that sustains them. (Gaüḍavaha 889)

Even when released from its mouth, the wicked sword bears a terrible nature; even for a moment when immersed in water, the blade retains its harshness. (Gaüḍavaho 890) [Āryā meter] For those who are doubly distressed by the fact that the excellence of their own virtues has been appropriated by another...
In truth, it is discernment alone that is the cause of the malice of the wicked.

Or rather, it is delusion, arising from a contempt for the virtues of others, that they claim virtues manifest themselves merely for the sake of their own self-importance; yet this is actually the cause of the greatness of those very virtues. (Gauḍavaho 891–892)
When they are expanded, even those things that are devoid of quality attain lightness;
how much more so, then, does that which is truly quality-less possess majesty? (Gaüḍavaho 893) [Āryā] [p.

In a matter concerning greatness and virtue, those who are not men of action desire the opposite arising of virtues, even when their own greatness is bound up with a matter of vice; for the pride born of virtue in noble men passes away from their hearts. (Gauḍavaho 894) [Āryā metre]

Therefore, as if unable to bear their pride, those virtues become heavy. (Gauḍavaho 895) And that very impurity of envy does not manifest clearly until discernment appears, and once the blessed fire has burned, the smoke has indeed subsided. (Gauḍavaho 896)
Upon seeing her from above, there is wonder; upon looking down at her, there is apprehension—just as for those looking up at a mountain and likewise for those looking down into a pit.
(Gauḍavaho 897) [Āryā meter] I desire to make myself free from all qualities, out of fear of being suspected by the malicious.
Like a garland of flowers tossed about by the agitation of venomous serpents at night, [so is the mind of the self-conceited].

(Gaüḍavaho 898) Even though the weight of his virtues is praised by the hearts of people, one who is proud of his own qualities, upon seeing those whose virtues have ascended to the world, swings himself back and forth among his own merits. (Gaüḍavaho 899)

Those endowed with virtue who have ascended to prosperity, and those prosperous ones possessed of great virtues, do not at all diminish one another, just as mountains do not diminish each other whether they are at their bases or their peaks. (Gaüḍavaha 900) [Āryā] [p.
Kings who possess great majesty do not become so full of pride toward those of truly great virtues as they are seen to be toward other kings.
As virtues diminish and faults ripen unhindered, [pride increases]. (Gauḍavaho 901) [Āryā metre]
If there were no one devoid of merit, even the entire world would likewise become empty of virtue.
(Gaüḍavaho 902) Or rather, what need is there for kings?
For even those who are free from all worldly desire and detached, such virtuous men become the attendants bound by the commands of Fate. (Gaüḍavaho 903)

Even when an undertaking has only just begun, it meets with destruction at its very peak, like a shipwrecked log in the ocean, solely through its own agitation; thus, the light of true knowledge alone reveals the lack of skill in those of base intellect. (Gauḍavaho 904) [Āryā]
This very radiance of his is like that of black sapphires.
(Gauḍavaho 905) Because of the vastness of their hearts, the intellects of the great do not manifest;
in great palaces, lamps with faint rays merely flicker. (Gauḍavaho 906)
Even through extreme separation, the intentions of the great do not waver;
like the flash of lightning, it bewilders the eyes because of its intensity. (Gauḍavaho 907) [Āryā] [p.
Those who acquire for themselves wealth are indeed not without grounds for pride;
yet those by whom poverty itself is acquired for themselves are truly something else. Some attain it, while others do not; they are seen to be different from one another. (Gauḍavaho 908) [Āryā metre]
Praise dwells between those who are base and those who are highly esteemed.

If he, enraged and distressed, should act perversely toward men of noble character who welcome death and have themselves abandoned their wealth, he would be acting like those of inferior nature. (Gauḍavaho 909–910)
Having become a mere attendant, she did not indeed attain the status of a queen;

yet, due to the fault of time, she did not even become an attendant to one who was heavy with virtues. I think that shadow was surely made for a youth who would come immediately after her. (Gauḍavaho 911) [Āryā]
Even in this burdened age of Kali, there is something that shines forth with stainless purity.
(Gaüḍavaho 912) What is the use of those houses where the doors are broken by the force of the arrows of Viśākha, and from which one departs filled with the joy of liberation? (Gaüḍavaho 913)
When she abandons her noble disposition, generosity, and compassion, and departs for some unknown place, the earth is struck by calamities. (Gaüḍavaho 914) [Āryā;

When even that which is easily obtained by others does not come to the great, they remain inwardly smiling in secret, filled with wonder; for the great show their acceptance of things to virtuous people only according to the weight of their own desire. (Gauḍavaho 915) [Āryā]

Like the reflection of great jewels seen through the medium of a mirror, so too do base men take pleasure in the company of noble people even when they are already under their own control; for those who possess easily obtained jewels, the mere wearing of them is indeed a sport. (Gauḍavaho 916–917)

How indeed can there be poverty for the great whose glory is established in their own strength? Yet, one miserly glory has gone to its very root and forgotten its origin. [Gaüḍavaho 918, Āryā meter] For misers who praise the virtue of giving in the domain of others...

In their own conduct, there was indeed no lack of enthusiasm, nor was there any lack of shame. Like a young bride accustomed to the company of her husband, Fortune herself became languid at their first union; otherwise, having attained glory, she would not have been so intent on amorous play. (Gauḍavaho 919–920)

The miserly, though not actually dying, wait for their wealth that has come within the range of their sight—wealth whose luster is as dark as a beloved woman’s face, like one who avoids a disease. (Gaüḍavaho 921) [Āryā;
Indeed, they consider even a mass of virtues heavy when it has reached its ultimate limit;
therefore, there is a conflict with prosperity, but not without cause regarding the virtues.
(Gaüḍavaho 922) [Āryā meter] The earth, commanded by the knitting of her brows, does not quickly support the burden of the entire host of men.
I think that Fortune, as she runs away in haste, stumbles along.

(Gaüḍavaho 923) Indeed, even for that most virtuous woman who has lost her husband, separation from him is considered by Fortune to be a destruction brought about by the power of destiny. (Gaüḍavaho 924)
How could there be a birth of Dharma for those who are like the Lord of Beings (Śiva) and true friends?
Prosperity is indeed unattainable for them, that source of fortune which dwells among the ignoble.
That prosperity which has long been born from vast lineages and which is ever radiant with its splendor— [Gaüḍavaho 925, Āryā meter].
It bestows knowledge upon those who have mastered it, yet not upon others;
it removes faults and bestows virtues.
This strange manifestation of Fortune appears to be something contradictory. (Gauḍavaho 926–927)
Those who enter the whirlpool of the battle against the tips of the circles of their enemies' weapons are indeed seized by the Fortune of Sovereignty in that very moment. (Gaüḍavaho 928) [Āryā;
Under the pretext of striking with their palms, men of pride who have long been accustomed to wielding the sword with one arm alone seem to ward off even their second arm through arrogance.
Virtues alone are the indicators of the Goddess of Fortune’s qualities, for Fortune herself does not exist apart from virtues.
One who desires fortune should cultivate virtues, for fortune does not come to those who lack virtues.

(Gaüḍavaho 930) It is established that virtues are the very root of the creeper of fortune; therefore, one must exert effort toward their increase, for by that alone does she ascend upward. (Gaüḍavaho 931)
How indeed can that fickle woman— by whom the feet of the honey-drinking god (Kāma) were first stumbled upon when he gave away his wealth to those who were disoriented, terrified,
and despondent— ever cause Fortune to bend before those resplendent with virtues? (Gauḍavaho 932) [Āryā]
My vision has been carried away by the darkness of the underworld for a long time. (Gauḍavaho 933) At the very commencement of which Fortune first stands, yet falters;
how indeed can she be won back through that same very petition? (Gauḍavaho 934)

The absence of suffering is not happiness; nor are those things happiness which are pleasures that must be abandoned. Only those things are truly happiness which are happinesses in themselves. (Gaüḍavaho 935) [Āryā] [p.
For those whose minds are solely intent on turning away from attachment to pleasure, there incessantly flashes forth the forest of the terrible miseries of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
whereas for those attached to pleasure, it is only through the increase of worldly objects that the density of its shadow is attained.
(Gauḍavaho 936) [Āryā meter] For those whose minds are solely intent on turning away from attachment to pleasure, it incessantly flashes forth.
Like the sound of a drum whose resonance is not cut off by the covering of fingers,
the hearts of great poets— having bestowed compassion through their compositions on the sentiments (*rasa*)— experience pleasure even while being tormented by their own sorrows. (Gauḍavaho 937–938)

Entering various [births] in this endless cycle of existence, those of steadfast heart regard families as mere temporary dwellings. Indeed, people find their suffering lightened by those very things that produce suffering. (Gauḍavaho 939) [Āryā]
Just as one might dispel exhaustion with cool breezes, so too,
under the guise of great joy, when the arms are raised at the reunion with kinsmen, the hearts surely overflow with tears that bring about their separation. (Gauḍavaho 940–941)

O fool! How could you have such laxity toward them, when you were bound so firmly by the moisture of their affection, and yet you now long for this transient world, having abandoned that which is eternal? (Gaüḍavaho 942) [Āryā] [p.
Alas, even when joined together without interval, the parts of the world become separated by vast distances, like the intervals between the ends of a loosened cord.
First, virtues do not exist for the sake of virtue; rather, they arise from that [substance] along with the virtues themselves. (Gauḍavaho 943) [Āryā]
Nowadays, there is only their reputation for virtue; alas, they themselves no longer exist.

(Gaüḍavaha 944) Due to the power of time, when the body of a virtuous man’s fame has met its destruction, only here and there do a few scattered fragments of his virtues remain, like bits of bone. (Gaüḍavaha 945)

Defects arising from firm habitual tendencies lead to bondage for those of base conduct, while the virtues of the truly noble lead to liberation; these do not cease until one attains direct knowledge.
This is detachment: that the heart finds delight even in fortunes as they come to pass. (Gauḍavaho 946) [Āryā metre]
But the scorn of Fortune indeed arises from a body that is ever-unstable and envious.
Is not that very king [the one who enjoys her]? For men, abandoning homes full of many deceptions, take delight in forest regions where waterfalls abound. (Gauḍavaho 947–948)

Is it that the very nature of the Pulinda people is a boon for service, or is it rather a curse? For such is the way of the world that even the inhabitants of the Vindhya forests are held in high regard. (Gauḍavaho 949) [Āryā;
The rivers with their various birds, the forests as pure as the ground, and the mountains resounding with the cries of elephants in rut—these all delight the eye;
yet, even if you are pure by nature, do not touch a person who is wretched. (Gaüḍavaho 950) [Āryā]
In that [state], only the misfortune that has emerged over time remains.
(Gaüḍavaha 951) Who else but the Creator is the author of those virtues of the wicked, by which even one's own self displays an indifference toward despondency? (Gaüḍavaha 952)
Surely even one's own beloved wife abandons a man whose fortune has vanished;
can the night ever unite with the moon when it is incomplete in all its parts?
O heart, you will suffer from the hope of attaining that which was proclaimed by others elsewhere.
It is better to be poor for one person than for the entire earth. (Gauḍavaho 954) Let alone the pride of rescuing the distressed; where could they find such weightiness?
Otherwise, they would not be able to do what is dear even to themselves among those who are not noble. (Gauḍavaho 955)

With their hearts utterly deluded by intense passion, having obtained wealth as if it were a virtue, how can they ever satisfy others when even their own selves are forgotten? (Gauḍavaho 956) [Āryā] [p.

Just as the world finds it difficult to enjoy even what is within its reach, so too some find it hard to obtain water cool to the touch; otherwise, those same waters would be different when they are in one's hand. (Gaüḍavaho 957) [Āryā] People with many virtues are rare, yet even a person possessing but a single virtue is not found everywhere.
We praise even the faultless for their rare virtues; indeed, even a slight blemish brings charm to common beauties.
Just as smoke, though undesirable, enhances the splendor of a great fire fueled by fragrant wood. (Gauḍavaho 958–959)

In the course of worldly affairs, true men possess only a few faults; otherwise, how could there be association with them, who are so extraordinary? As for those whose excellence is not even known, what state of virtue can they possibly possess? (Gaüḍavaho 960) [Āryā metre]
Even by transgressing his former good conduct, he does not thereby become virtuous;

nevertheless, those very same faults that were heard and known when he was silent are still perceived even while he speaks, and those very same virtues that were known when he was silent are still known even while he lives. (Gauḍavaho 961–962)
Seek your own shadow in the world through conduct alone; what is the use of external ornaments?
For a jewel does not break when it is outside its setting. (Gauḍavaho 963) [Āryā] [p.

There are those who possess equal virtues and faults and display only their defects; there are those who are averse to both virtues and faults and experience only their flaws; but there are none who take up only the measure of virtue. Someone appears as if indifferent, yet in his heart he is pure. (Gauḍavaho 964) [Āryā meter]
The mango fruit has been stolen, and the cow has reached the ultimate state of digestion.
(Gaüḍavaho 965) Even if someone appears stainless in some matter and is thus peerless, nevertheless, his reddish-yellow beard is common with the color of saffron. (Gaüḍavaho 966)

Virtuous people praise even a person whose entire collection of qualities is marred by falsehood, provided they are free from envy; for who would disparage a jewel because it is covered by mud? (Gaüḍavaho 967) [Āryā meter] The state of being free from fault shines, provided that the quality [of freedom from envy] has emerged from the weeds of jealousy.
Even when one stands amidst virtues, egoism causes distress, as if amidst riches.
Therefore, we bow to those riches which are honored for their qualities and yet devoid of even a fraction of wealth; let it be by such riches alone that we are honored. (Gaüḍavaho 968–969)

Even when destitute of material wealth, the virtuous find contentment through this much alone: that by means of even a fraction of their own virtues, they grant some small measure of joy. (Gaüḍavaha 970) [Āryā] [p.
The faces of the virtuous, whose joy has vanished at the time of giving, burn with shame;
their eyes see only emptiness when they look upon the recipient in his agitation.
(Gaüḍavaha 971) [Āryā] Alas, the hearts of those who are consumed by heavy anxiety hang down with their faces turned downward.

How can those whose minds are uplifted have any vain efforts? (Gaüḍavaho 972) In the past they gave as much as they desired; then, when others stopped giving, they took from others out of necessity; and thereafter, they seized [wealth] through the lure of greed. (Gaüḍavaho 973)
In a world where the true essence is unknown, the virtues of the great, though established by their own discernment, flourish only for a brief moment as they rise up.
Let him take his wealth; let him cast aside his name, his playful charms, and the graceful movements of his youth. (Gauḍavaho 974) [Āryā]
"Alas! How does fate torment hearts that are overflowing with virtues?
(Gaüḍavaho 975) "Just as the fame of the great becomes firmly rooted, even though it is unsupported by anything else and is shattered by its own weight," (Gaüḍavaho 976)

Upon the acquisition of wealth, during its transformation, and at its destruction, even those few instances of impropriety regarding riches and pleasures bring about a change of heart. (Gauḍavaho 977) [Āryā] [p.
Thinking, "My own virtues do not tolerate being placed before the great," the inferior qualities, in their pursuit of the lowly, steal away the very essence of those virtues.
A wicked person is indeed unspeakable; through false praise, he makes the villain twice as much so. (Gauḍavaho 978) [Āryā]

Even a good friend, when his virtues have declined, becomes malicious in both ways. (Gaüḍavaho 979) Even that which he says out of affection—"He is no different from myself"—the villain establishes as a matter of fact through the course of events; it is nothing but malice. (Gaüḍavaho 980)

Even while wearing the most brilliant ornaments of poetry, the ear perceives that the particular essence of the wealth of learning is the head-ornament (the crest-jewel). (Gaüḍavaho 981) [Āryā] Fortune is not fickle toward those who are highly esteemed; yet it is they alone who abandon her when she does so.
If they nevertheless abandon that very same [wealth], what fault is there in her? (Gauḍavaho 982) Thirst remains unbroken even when wealth has perished;
even after reaching a mountain and climbing it, how could one have ascended the sky? (Gauḍavaho 983)

I think that, in the presence of Fortune who is fond of the mud, the miserly lords create, as it were, a lotus pond by means of the pretext of their folded palms joined in salutation. (Gauḍavaho 984) [Āryā;
It is said that even by the mountains, with their trees stripped of flowers and fruits and their birds driven away, the ocean was not abandoned as it entered it;
for those who exert themselves when the arrival of pleasure or pain is near reach the fruit of their efforts. (Gaudavaho 985) [Āryā metre]

May the adventitious calamities of those who, through the influence of the serpent of delusion, long search for their lost glory, come to an end— just as there is no scratching for Fate when the itch of his brow is already satisfied by its own thought. (Gauḍavaho 986–987)
Even for those adorned with noble conduct, misfortunes indeed arise through the decree of fate;
yet I consider them to be accompanied by their wives, since they maintain their dignity through a heart that does not despond. (Gauḍavaho 988) [Āryā]

A wicked person, failing to reach that uneven ground, becomes a burden to his elders. (Gaüḍavaho 989) In this very world, for the sake of pacifying the heart, the fruit of which has already been attained, there is no confidence in the forest-dwelling of the next world, whose fruit is yet to come. (Gaüḍavaho 990)
The wealthy man delights in excellence; one who possesses only a small fortune takes pride in mere stability;
the poor man desires his very body; and the wretched man finds satisfaction in life itself. (Gauḍavaho 991) [Āryā] [p.
At first dense at the base and then thinning out in their upward flow, the continuations of stories even by the wise eventually fade away in the course of time. Obstacles,
becoming thick within the heart, cause one to falter when they turn unpleasant.

Those who are accustomed to a life of ease, being filled with the burden of pleasure, hear [this] through their lack of experience. (Gaüḍavaho 993) Even when things have become tasteless, that fickleness of the heart which cannot be turned back by any means—toward that, people here fall into delusion. (Gaüḍavaho 994)
In the hearts of young women, firmly fixed within their breasts, both intellects—those directed toward this world and those toward the other world—are placed together as one.
How indeed does the bodiless god strike? How indeed do his flower-arrows pierce? (Gauḍavaho 995) [Āryā]

How can those very same sensual pleasures, when unattained, bring happiness? For the heart, this is its very hardness; what need is there to establish it? Within women themselves, the essence of breasts dwells as nothing but hardness. (Gauḍavaho 996–997)
The world delights in conduct that is not fully blossomed, grieves over its own character, censures the nature of others, and boasts of the virtues of others. (Gauḍavaho 998) [Āryā;
The long, white tresses of people appear like a path as they pass by daily, following the course of the heart's inclinations.
(Gaüḍavaho 999) [Āryā] Surely the entire arrangement of her limbs reveals the river through its folds.

In this body, the state of being a skeleton due to old age is imminent. (Gaüḍavaho 1000) Bowed down by all its strength, dragged down by the creepers of wrinkles, this body now hangs as if toward the surface of the earth. (Gaüḍavaho 1001)
As if worn out by the ripening of the dense drops of sweat falling upon her limbs, her hair appears, under the guise of sesame seeds, as if possessing a dark luster.
Thus was she seen by her husband, whose mind was longing for his wife who had reached youth beyond the stage of maidenhood. (Gauḍavaho 1002) [Āryā]

The milk flows forth from the udders as if it were a solid mass due to the density of the streams of milk. (Gauḍavaho 1003) [Āryā] Because of its quality of being unpleasant at the time of cessation, everything is indeed suffering;
there is no such thing as happiness that is not suffering, nor is there any suffering that does not contain happiness. (Gauḍavaho 1004) [Āryā]
The sky clearly manifests its nature as "non-existence" under the guise of the world;
it is like the blueness of the firmament revealed through observation. (Gaüḍavaho 1005) [Āryā] [p.

May the fruit of your dwelling in this tasteless cycle of existence—the realization of the Lord’s virtues through constant contemplation—emerge as a priceless gain for you sinners. Furthermore— GaüḍVa. 1006 [Āryā]—and also:

Defeated by the luster of his dark throat that extends as far as the horizon, that very mass of loose matted hair assumes the appearance of a mane; it bears the radiance falling from the hoods placed upon his head, which are colored by the rays of his jewels. (Gauḍavaho 1007) [Āryā]
The lord of beasts has his long tail obstructed by the mass of [his own] back;
from the depths of the cavities of his mouths, which are wide open in secret, his rows of flames attain the beauty of a garland of crest-jewels. (Gauḍavaho 1008–1009)
Those very rays, having become cool like moonlight on the path of the statues and having descended upon the faces of the sky, go forth and assume the state of celestial goads in his hands.
Thus, by the Three-Eyed One, whose power and majesty were weighed against that of Mahiṣa, [he was subdued]. (Gauḍavaho 1010) [Āryā metre]
The physician’s cowrie-treasure, having been transformed into the form of a tiger— by him,
on the field of battle, the trunks of the enemy’s elephants were severed like venomous serpents that have shed their tongues and streams of blood from their nostrils. (Gauḍavaho 1011–1012)
The great column of smoke from the sacrificial fire of this lord of the gods, who has become a performer of noble deeds,
resembles the path of the celestial elephant, dark with its thick ichor. (Gauḍavaho 1013) [Āryā meter]

By him, those who were lightened by the weight of their lack of virtue and heavy due to the pride of their own lineage were made heavy once again through the pride of their own selves— [he who, though bound by the duty of his lord, spoke contrary words].
(Gaüḍavaho 1014) [Āryā metre] For one established in the bond of the master’s dharma, even a wife who speaks perversely...
Accompanied by sighs of compassion, they endure the frowns of fury; or rather, it is seen by the lord of tortoises with his conch-jewel shell raised up. (Gaüḍavaho 1015) [Āryā metre]
Like the ocean whose waves were seized in agitation by the gods,
the sea was leaped over by Kamaṭhanātha with the undulating ripples of his back, even though his body was weakened by long-held sighs of exhaustion. (Gauḍavaho 1016–1017)
Resembling clouds with visible cranes, flashing repeatedly like lightning,

their throats red from being seen while gasping for breath— these great fish, as vast and white as the path of the earth joined together, are beheld by the gods and the Daityas. (Gauḍavaho 1018) [Āryā metre]
The back of the Lord of the Tortoise, dark by its very nature as far as the edge, is seen in the ocean with a form undulating like breaking waves. (Gaüḍavaho 1019) [Āryā] [p. 151]
Like the reflection of a mountain in a jeweled casket possessing an abundance of flavors;
With their branches bent by the pressure of the coiled serpent-bracelets and drooping low, the masses of trees—joined like mountains at their tops—break apart at their roots. (Gauḍavaho 1020–1021)

The forest-thicket groves, which serve as play-grounds for the claws of the Lord of Birds, are being torn apart upon the chest of the Lord of Beasts by the sharp, rending talons; meanwhile, the trees burst open, their perimeters encircled by the spreading spray of dust. (Gauḍavaho 1022) [Āryā]
The banks of the rivers have their slopes struck down at the time of their reversal; the rows of sprouts are destroyed as the water flows away from the mountains that have collapsed.
Even though they were once slender, the mountain streams have reached a state of vastness as their banks crumble and fall, cut off by the waters of the rivers descending from the crumbling hills.

The masses of water, whose roots at the broad base were loosened and uprooted, were carried away by those very first slender streams; their bases were shattered by the friction of the lords of serpents as they emerged from the openings.
Exhausted by resting and moving slowly, they fell from a great distance after being severed from the mountains. (Gauḍavaho 1025) [Āryā meter]
Gradually, small cascades form circles as they descend; their roots are slender, and they strike against the slopes of mountains that are broad at the base.
(Gaüḍavaha 1026) [Āryā meter, p. 152] pāvantivalia-vitthaa-giri-kaḍaa-ṇihaṁsaṇā taliṇa-mūlā.
The lords of the elephants of the quarters, with their circles of tusks extended wide, [roared].
Just as the lord of the serpents, having crushed and drained the trees, coils himself upon the mountain, so too does the long-tailed one again twist around the mountain. (Gauḍavaho 1027–1028)
The ocean, its surrounding expanse bound by dust from the moisture dried up by the friction of the serpent’s hood,

appears like a lake whose mud has momentarily ceased to settle. (Gauḍavaho 1029) [Āryā] Upon the serpent’s hood, which has attained the appearance of a lotus, as the waves vanish at the receding shore due to the friction of the serpent’s hood...
Those who do not depart enter mountain caves like cities devoid of people.

(Gaüḍavaho 1030) Due to the nature of the mountain’s slopes, the paths of the falling boulders—though straight and striking against ridges that join various directions—appear as if they were crooked. (Gaüḍavaho 1031)
The echo, its expansion obstructed by the circle of the quarters and the sky filled with leaping spray,
clings only momentarily to the ocean itself. [Gaüḍavaha 1032] Arising from the friction of the wind and emerging from the hollows of the forest thickets where the wings were torn away—
Mountain ridges fall down, shattered by the impact of thunderbolt-like torrents;
bodies are dragged out, being whirled about within the turning circles of the ocean.
The excellent elephant-kings, with their trunks relaxed and curved like the coils of a serpent, [trample the mountains];

the rivers, whose waters are held back on the paths of the sandalwood forests that have been cleared away, possess the beauty of trees bent by the creepers and the splendor of mountain peaks. (Gauḍavaho 1034–1035)
As if pushed into the sky by the mountain peaks themselves, the earth has now settled against the very base of the mountain,
its middle portion thinned by friction against the quarters of the horizon.
With its foundation established upon the back of a tortoise, its lower part thinned by the friction of the lord of serpents.
With great difficulty, the mountain that had been first placed there was gently removed.

(Gaüḍavaho 1037) The earth’s circumference, which had been scorched by the shattering of Mount Mandara and moistened by the agitated ocean, was restored as a cooling remedy upon the surface of the underworld. (Gaüḍavaho 1038)
Even now, the Goddess of Fortune—who was hastily borne by the ocean of milk when it was agitated and abandoned by Kama—is still supported by him upon his chest; she is nourished by him.
Furthermore—

Her breast is seen, darkened by the blood trickling from wounds caused by the slapping of her hands, as if stained by the smoke of the fire of separation dwelling within her heart. (Gauḍavaho 1040) [Āryā;

In the absence of the rays from the crest-jewels on the heads of the elephants, which were obstructed as they were driven by the goads, there fell thick streams of tears, stainless and free from collyrium;
these were gathered for a mere moment when obstructed by the dense garlands of hanging lotus-stalks. (Gauḍavaho 1041) [Āryā]
Sighs are emitted from the hollows of his cheeks as they are whirled around.
(Gaüḍavaho 1042) When his brow was made uneven by the emergence of playful anger, the limbs of the wives of his enemies—distraught at the loss of their husbands—trembled. (Gaüḍavaho 1043)
He whose belly, through the interior of the world entered by the wind from his mouth,
vomits forth the mass of other Brahma-eggs with five colors— that Eka-Keśava,
who has measured the expanse of the ocean with his unbridled arms, [is victorious]. (Gauḍavaho 1044) [Āryā metre]
Then he sat down upon the merchant’s seat, which was as if the very remainder of his own glory;
or rather,
by means of the stars— those masses of light capable of bearing the burden of the sky— he illuminated the expanse of the heavens.
She shines with her two lotus-feet joined together like those of the remaining infants;

she bears a pair of feet whose luster is like that of abundant red lac, appearing as if the glow of jewels were clinging to them from their resting upon the circle of hoods of the lord of serpents. (Gauḍavaho 1046–1047)
The royal swans, resounding with the jingling of anklets from their feet playfully tossed about, appear as if they were the coils of the serpent Śeṣa’s hoods being raised up. (Gaüḍavaho 1048) [Āryā]

Bearing the shadow of the filaments of her girdle, which are darkened by the pollen clinging to the bees that hover about her, she wears a mass of rays as a girdle-string; she is being served by the reflection of her own jeweled girdle as it bounces back against her. (Gauḍavaho 1049) [Āryā]
As if by a people engaged in the labor of uprooting the mountain Rōhaṇa, [the earth was shaken];
through the opening of her navel, which was like the tusk of the Boar of Causes, she bore the underworld, where the line of hair appeared like emerging darkness. (Gauḍavaho 1050–1051)
Even now, she reveals her waist— uneven with the furrows of her folds, beautiful as the earth, and appearing like the rutting-path left by the departure of Rāma,
whose beauty remains unblemished— and she shines with the wave of a line of body-hairs that undulates like a string of pearls. (Gauḍavaho 1052) [Āryā meter]
With her waist like the middle of the Ganges' current where it meets the Yamunā;
(1053) She appeared as if displaying a cluster of trees with their roots revealed within, by means of the chowries held aloft by her attendants, which were shimmering with her own loveliness. (1054)
She reveals, as it were, a second lake whose waters have overflowed its banks due to the mass of horripilation caused by the moisture of the nectar of the sight of her lord. (Gauḍavaho 1055) [Āryā]

And her breast-mirror was covered with tears that fell upon the image [of her husband], like water settling within a pond that has no outlet; meanwhile, swarms of bees repeatedly alighted and flew away from the flowers on her neck. (Gauḍavaho 1056) [Āryā metre]
Like a script written upon limbs exhausted by exertion, yet once more with the aid of medicinal herbs;
like divine cities possessing the quality of having their circular perimeters reached by the limits of pearls, it was endowed with the splendor of jeweled earrings. (Gauḍavaho 1057–1058)

She displays her face-disk, as golden-white as Mount Sumeru, which has become dark-blue at night due to the tresses resting between the earrings, the moon, and the sun; with every limb touched by the staff-like rays of her pearl necklace on all sides. (Gaüḍavaho 1059, Āryā meter)
She appears as if she possesses a multitude of stainless, opened lotus-petals;
she bears her cheeks, whose roots are marked by drops of nectar trickling from the flowers on her ears, as if they were shedding the remaining residue of pollen. (Gauḍavaho 1060–1061)
[The city] possesses fragrant tresses of hair formed by garland-wreaths, as if they were the braided locks of bees, betraying the presence of many rival kings. (Gaüḍavaho 1062) [Āryā metre]
It is heard that he indeed repeatedly and directly consoles the goddess Earth— who is settled within his own body—
during her sufferings.
Furthermore:

Even today, his own reflection—marked by a dark spot emerging from the pursuit of the stars as if it were a crest-jewel—surpasses his two eyes in splendor. In the lineage of that lord, the lover of the night, was formerly established... [Gauḍavaho 1064, Āryā meter]
If this is my salutation to them, yet something more has emerged. (Gauḍavaho 1065) [Āryā] Furthermore—
she emerges with her face turned away, bewildered by the dawning of both terror and remorse.
In the intervals between her eyelashes, which were becoming sparse as she smiled at the sight of him;
with her sprout-like hand, she rested upon her swaying breast-circle, where the rays of her nails were streaming across her heart as it moved back and forth toward him. (Gauḍavaho 1066–1067)
The trembling caused by the clashing of jeweled bells upon her firm hips makes the garland of flowers on her neck sway across her body. (Gauḍavaho 1068) [Āryā;
Before him, the amorous gestures of rival princesses—who had prepared their beds for marriage—become filled with trepidation.
Amidst the mass of rays emerging from the emeralds of his armlets, he perceives himself... [Gaüḍavaho 1069, Āryā meter].
She is like the Goddess Lakṣmī, longing for the lotus grove, who departs from him;
meanwhile, the mass of darkness, like a family of serpents with the jewels of their hoods in the form of stars, advances toward the circle of the forest of the submarine fire.
"O Lord of the Earth, we are witnesses to his virtuous conduct;
even the thousand heads of that serpent [Śeṣa], though they have no limit, are not heard to be sufficient for it.
Nevertheless, O King, listen to this mirror of the pride of his arms. (Gauḍavaho 1072) [Āryā]
Only at the end of the night is the extermination of the former kings of Pūri being reported;
this slaughter of the Gauḍas, a great undertaking, is now being accomplished by me, in which both kings and monkey-lords alike lose their pride upon hearing of it. (Gauḍavaho 1073–1074)
But now, the orb of the sun, its mass of rays dispersed, rolls away with a reddish-brown hue like that of a tortoise-shell turned over. (Gauḍavaho 1075) [Āryā;

These forest borders, resounding with the joyous cries of lions sleeping in mountain thickets, are being entered by pigeons bright with shifting shadows. [Gaüḍavaha 1076] [Āryā] It is being embraced by the rays of the Lord of Day scattered from mountains whose peaks have been struck.
The earth is encircled by the rivers' paths of shadow, as if by streams of molten iron.

(Gaüḍavaho 1077) In these rivers, where the masses of birds have gathered together without interval, the expanses of the sandbanks, freed from the obstruction of the swirling water, seem to overflow in circular eddies. (Gaüḍavaho 1078)

In the city streets, the ends of day become grey like the sun at sunset, with cattle returning from afar for the first time; they move with slow, expansive steps, their heavy hips languidly descending.
(Gauḍavaho 1079) [Āryā] They approach with slightly broadened gait, their heavy hips moving slowly.
The forest edges are white with milch cows and thick with *paṇhua* flowers.
Having rolled up one half of its body at the start of the day and retreated, the Vindhya mountain now spreads out the second half as a circle of shadow. (Gauḍavaho 1080–1081)
The Fortune of Day swings upon the ridges of the western mountain, while the garlands of the sun’s rays grow reddish with the lines of knots in withered lotus stalks. (Gauḍavaho 1082) [Āryā] [p.
The courtyards of the mansions, now solitary with the windows empty because those standing behind have departed, appear beautiful with their clearly visible outlines.
Their interiors are made vast by the gaps appearing through the roots of the sunbeams as they enter from the side. (Gauḍavaho 1083) [Āryā]
The forest regions, their density loosened by the emergence of shadows, become sparse;

split by the cutting of mountain peaks, they rise high according to the expansion of the sun and, bowing down, enter into a state of being the refuge for those oppressed by the heat. (Gauḍavaho 1084–1085)

In this day, which is like a lion’s roar at the time of the householder’s release from bondage, the sun and moon act as jars filled with blood that has trickled and remained; and when the meal of the sun has been consumed by the wine of twilight in the mouth of Yama’s messenger.

*Gaüḍavaha* 1086 [Āryā] The sun and moon act as jars filled with blood that has trickled and remained, during this day that is like a lion’s roar at the time of the householder’s release from bondage; and when the meal of the sun has been consumed by the wine of twilight in the mouth of Yama’s messenger.
The stars, like blossoms, are being nibbled by the jagged tips of the lion’s mane.
(Gaüḍavaho 1087) At the end of the day, the orb of the sun—reddish like the corner of an exhausted buffalo’s eye—is turning pale, like the interior of a *kalamba* bud on the earth. (Gaüḍavaho 1088)
When the solar disc has been seized by twilight, as if by a cloth, the thick shadow of night emerges like a streak of smoke from a bed of fire. (Gauḍavaho 1089) [Āryā;

The orb of the sun appears like a mass of smoke, jagged with rays reddened and clouded by its accumulation; it resembles the dark, fresh blood dripping from the throat of a great buffalo, as it merges with the uneven twilight clouds that are being swallowed by the onset of darkness.
(Gauḍavaho 1090) [Āryā] It possesses the splendor of the dark, fresh blood flowing from the throat of a great buffalo.

The masses of darkness, kissing the solar orb of the rising mango tree, are overcome by the sun; and the sun, his body turned tawny by the advancing darkness along with its chariot and horses, acquires the luster of the Garuḍa whose feathers bristle with pride at the slayer of Madhu. (Gauḍavaho 1091–1092)
When the sun has set on the mountain, its rays becoming pale-red like mountain dust,

the day’s shadow— brownish-yellow like a crab— whirls about as it merges with the gathering darkness. With the trees upon the mountain peaks serving as nests for their own hands-like branches, the solar orb [is hidden].
The twilight falls like a mass of clouds shattered by the downpour of the rainy season.

(Gauḍavaho 1094) The evening elephant, its palate at the edge of the sky reddened by twilight as indicated by its slight turning back, devours the orb of the sun like a morsel of food. (Gauḍavaho 1095)
The sky, encircled by the wide halo of the intensely risen twilight, bears a shadow as vast as the broad, fallen orb of the setting sun. (Gaüḍavaho 1096) [Āryā;
The sky—where the darkness of the quarters has vanished and the solar disc rests upon the western horizon—is glowing like Garuḍa clutching a mountain and a tortoise;
it casts aside the great boar of darkness as Mount Sumeru would be pushed away. (Gauḍavaho 1097) [Āryā]
The twilight, with the rays of the sun like its trailing filaments, is like a lotus stalk.
When the solar disc, marked by its first flush of dawn, has been cast into the wide stalk of the sky’s splendor, the moon emerges like a second bulbous root. (Gauḍavaho 1098–1099)

The cities of the Gandharvas, straightened by the onset of the downpour and grey with the stalks of the palm groves, become cloudless as the sun’s orb sets; the remaining streaks of the sun’s rays form a support for the staff-like [remnants of the sky]. (Gauḍavaho 1100) [Āryā metre]
The western quarter of the world-palace is being set ablaze by the fire.
(Gaüḍavaha 1101) The mass of darkness, dark-blue as it encircles the sky and the earth, rolls in the midst like a cluster of date-palm trunks, variegated by the remnants of twilight. (Gaüḍavaha 1102)

In every direction, the streaks of darkness appear turbid with a mass of clusters of stars, like the Yamunā river rushing in haste at the onset of her agitation over the falling of the sun. (Gaüḍavaha 1103) [Āryā;

In the evening, the quarters of the sky, filled with circles of darkness emerging from the setting sun, meet together like female elephants whose own state of pregnancy is made manifest by their proximity [to the moon].
(Gauḍavaho 1104) [Āryā meter] Someone [has seen it], marked by the root of the dark, reddish vine of twilight as it sighs...
The orb of the moon, like a golden vessel, lifts itself up from the sky as if it were a copper cauldron.
(Gaüḍavaho 1105) As if drawn forth by the curiosity of the talk concerning the Lord of the Earth, the quarters of the sky, grey with the hue of evening's end, meet together. (Gaüḍavaho 1106)
The thickets of light from the moon, having barely cleared the peaks of darkness that gape wide with density,
cause even the dry uplands to be suspected as caves by those who see but little.
The light of the moon spreads forth, severed from its entry into the shadows.
The sky appears like a path variegated with dark-colored streaks spreading from the stains of impurity;
its skull-like fragments are scattered and sparse due to the falling of the stars, and it is as decrepit as an old, decayed leather bag. (Gauḍavaho 1108–1109)

The quarters of the sky, though the evening has arrived, appear as if their darkness were thin, for they are obscured by the emergence of columns of smoke rising slowly from the sacrificial fires. (Gauḍavaho 1110) [Āryā;
The sky, dark with the massing gloom gathered amidst the light of the obscured moon and sun, resembles a sword rendered stainless by the stream of blood from a severed head;
at its horizons, it bears the likeness of a lotus whose filaments are slightly moistened by the lingering darkness. (Gauḍavaho 1111) [Āryā meter]
The sky, possessing the hue of saffron from the garments of the bride-like twilight, has become radiant;
the rising Garuda of the sun casts his discus into the sky like a vessel of nectar, extinguishing the fire of twilight with a multitude of drops from the clusters of planets. (Gauḍavaho 1112–1113)
Behold the orb of the night-maker, appearing like a mass of ripe *māhava* fruit, with its circle of moonlight made manifest by the emergence of the swarms of bees that are the shadows.
(Gaüḍavaho 1114) [Āryā meter] It is lifted up by the beam of the scale of the sky, its horn-like hand rising upward.
Later, by bearing the mass of the sun’s rays, he became like a water-jar marked with the moon.

(Gaüḍavaho 1115) The deer-marked one (the moon), turned pale-red by the agitation born from being summoned as an assistant for Love, goes forth like a circle of a bow drawn under the pretext of its surrounding halo. (Gaüḍavaho 1116)
The lord of the night has become copper-red like a ripe pāpava fruit, with his thin streaks of darkness slipping away and loosened;
he is like a drunken elephant whose dark-blue garment has slipped off. (Gauḍavaho 1117) [Āryā] [p.

Moreover— the bimba fruit of the Lord of Night, red as a conch-shell and a navel, bursts forth as if it had obtained its royal consecration from the jar of honey brought by the Kāminīs at that very moment. (Gauḍavaho 1118) [Āryā]
"The autumnal elephant, having uprooted the hanging lotus stalks with haste under the delusion that they were lotuses, sighs because of his trembling trunk.
Having spoken thus,
he, leaning upon his couch, [described] the deeds of the gods...
In the matter of reporting, the soul feels as if it were incompetent.
(Gauḍavaho 1120) The very glories of the great ones inspire one to perform what ought to be done;
yet those same glories, through such a report, cause the hearts to grow weary. (Gauḍavaho 1121)
Indeed, what activities have begun to proceed?
Love pierces the excellent lover with arrows that are filaments; for the purpose of the arrows of other people, he makes the flowers his targets. (Gaüḍavaha 1122) [Āryā]

Even though it has attained its full breadth through the cleansing of the newly applied brow and forehead, her face—possessing a pair of wide eyes with exceptionally bright pupils—is radiant. Adorned with earrings and ornaments, the women captivate the heart. (Gauḍavaha 1123) [Āryā] Vīābharaṇāya-karṇa-maṇḍanā adhiharanti ramaṇīyo.
Like *sahakāra* creepers empty within despite their flowers and fruits; having taken various bird-feathers as dye, they possess the luster of *añjana*, fish-roe, and *mañjarī* blossoms.
The multitude of amorous women appears like a collection of paintings completed by the Painter;
under the guise of a mass of smoke from the burning black aloe-wood incense, she seems to have embraced the darkness out of joy at the arrival of her lover. (Gauḍavaho 1125–1126)

The thighs of the women have become slightly swollen from the application of sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains, yet they remain capable of supporting their heavy hips; their breasts, though firm, appear to be melting away at the neck while remaining fresh upon the head. (Gauḍavaho 1127) [Āryā]
Even when worn at the same time, the floral ornaments of young women appear uneven;

for the forest bridegroom approaches, wearing as his excellent ornament a dark-blue net-like veil covering the impressions on his breasts, like armor held over his heart out of fear of Cupid’s arrows. (Gauḍavaho 1128–1129)
In the evening, the couple shines, having prepared their finery for the day of reunion;
they are eager for the arrival of the royal elephant and the sun’s rays, respectively.
(Gaüḍavaha 1130) [Āryā] Even she, whose broad golden girdle and bracelets have slipped down from her swelling breasts...
To the lover, whose limbs are unsteady from the agony of separation, it appears like a rampart of fire kindled by the fear of the god of love.
(Gauḍavaho 1131) [Āryā] [p. 167] It cannot be endured by the amorous man, whose body is distraught by the pangs of parting.
Like the moon’s web of rays upon entering the orb of the sun,
the limbs of amorous women— though wasting away, their strength abandoned by the longing of love for a beloved difficult to attain— have become heavy. (Gaüḍavaho 1132–1133)

Moreover— her gaze, with its eyebrows raised as if to brush away the sprout-like ears that obstructed it, and with the lashes of her eyes quivering due to the constraint of her knitting brows, gazes upward. (Gauḍavaho 1134) [Āryā]

The eyes of the bashful women do not indeed turn toward the actor, even when his throat-garlands are crushed by their hands; their lashes are turned upward and kiss the lids. Their hands move about, having cast aside the placement of their restless glances at the moment of his appearance. (Gauḍavaho 1135) [Āryā]
Like ears seized by the arrow-like contact of her eyes, [the gazes of the women remain fixed].

(Gauḍavaho 1136) Even as they depart, their glances—marked by words spoken with suppressed shame and with lips slightly parted as they smile—are cast back toward them, for their waists are bent. (Gauḍavaho 1137)
For these women, whose passion blossoms at the union with their beloveds, their playful gestures become imbued with a sentiment restrained by timidity. (Gauḍavaho 1138) [Āryā] [p.
The playful lotus-fiber ornaments of the women approach the beloveds without hesitation at night, like the rays of the moon, the lord of the captive elephants. Their eyelashes,
which resemble garlands of fresh sprouts reddened by wine, are like the petals of a blooming lotus.
The eyes of lovers bloom as if for the sake of entering into dalliance.
(Gaüḍavaho 1140) The eyes of a certain woman become streaked with lines of tears, as if she were bound by chains out of fear of departing from her beloved, who had been slighted.
(Gaüḍavaho 1141)
Even by a slight [insult] she is distressed, yet she does not accept even a heavy charm of his name;
thus, through her affection, the hearts of young women become inconsistent.
(Gaüḍavaha 1142) [Āryā meter] Of those proud women whose moon-like faces are turned upward with their cheeks blooming...

The mass of laughter, suppressed within, appears as if bursting forth. (Gaüḍavaha 1143) In the mirror of her face, which is slightly lowered by the upward-turning lotus-like eyes made light by the weight of her sighs, a certain woman, heavy with the pride of her remaining [beauty], looks back for a long time. (Gaüḍavaha 1144)
Some woman, her limbs withered by passion as she emerged from the secret place, drinks the honey with her heart as if with a lotus stalk. (Gauḍavaha 1145) [Āryā] [p.
Long established, he now becomes agitated; long separated, he now breaks apart;
in the midst of the assembly of women intoxicated by wine, he plays with a perverse passion.
His body and speech are unimpeded, yet his heart naturally loses its fortitude as the intoxication subsides.
The young women are known to be intoxicated solely by the glow upon their cheeks.
(Gaüḍavaha 1147) Though their limbs are delicate, the playful intoxication of honey makes them seem somehow heavy;
yet it lightens the hearts of their lovers, even though those hearts are burdened by pride. (Gaüḍavaha 1148)
In the union with their beloveds, the sighs of women—remaining as if they had escaped from the pain of separation, lingering in their hearts, and released from their mouths—are beautiful.
The full orb-like breasts of the young women [shine] upon the paths of the fresh night-sky. (Gauḍavaho 1149) [Āryā]
The embrace of beautiful women, whose breasts are roughened by the lines of the sky, endures as if bursting with the secret, eager sighs of joy at the union with a beloved.
Even the embrace of a woman whose breasts are like the moon, though it possesses the fragrance of jasmine,
produces a flavor that excels the joy of attaining the God of Love.

The first pressing of the breasts, caused by the heart being oppressed by the weight of longing for a firm embrace, was experienced by someone whose heart was pained by that burden. (Gauḍavaho 1152) [Āryā;

Even for those whose passion for the first stirrings of love has not yet begun, their limbs become so pressed against the chest of the child that they are rendered continuous with her hips; thus, through excessive intoxication, the hearts of the wanton women become empty as if drained. (Gauḍavaho 1153) [Āryā]
As the days grow increasingly devoid of flavor, the nights alone approach with true delight.

(Gaüḍavaha 1154) Couples, whose hearts were previously disregarded by pleasure as it faltered during moments of mutual longing, now attain a bliss even greater through the expansion of their amorous play. (Gaüḍavaha 1155)
When passion has fully blossomed, they offer the juice of the *tāliñca* fruit;

the amorous sports of women, radiant with the ornaments of nail-marks bestowed by their lovers, steal away the fatigue of couples whose bodies are pressed together without interval by the weight of their words. (Gauḍavaho 1156) [Āryā] It takes away the weariness of the pairs of lovers whose bodies are closely pressed together by the weight of their conversation.
Even upon her feet, he performed the grace of embracing all her limbs;
Upon the breast-dishes of many women, broad with the fullness attained by youth, his thrill of horripilation became like a single, rare streak. (Gauḍavaho 1157–1158)
A certain smiling woman, with her hand made pure, gently rubbed the chest of her lover, which was slightly raised as it pressed against her firm, swelling breasts. (Gauḍavaho 1159) [Āryā] [p.

The slender-waisted young woman is burdened by her circle of breasts, which have become heavy with the powder from the tips of her lover’s nails, broken again and again; while her arms are cast across her hips, drawn near by her bosom which has been bent down by the thinness of her waist. (Gauḍavaho 1160) [Āryā]

The beloved’s face, with its beautiful curved eyebrows, shone as it rested upon her thighs that were marked by folds; her cheeks were moistened by drops of perspiration arising from the fatigue of sleep, and she was gently rocked back and forth by the lover who, fearing her awakening, kissed her softly. (Gauḍavaho 1161–1162)
In sleep, the group of young women has their limbs lying relaxed and exhausted as they breathe with evenness, appearing somewhat frail; yet, O King,
this is only because they have been released by the gods who were waiting for an opportunity to speak of your valor.
A mass of stars falls from the sky like a cluster of flowers;
the orb of the lord of stars has become pale with rays like white lotus stalks, its halo reddish-yellow like the broken pieces of a ripe jambu fruit. (Gauḍavaho 1164–1165)
When the darkness, like a hand of hair, has been washed away by the morning dew, the stars fall like drops of water from the young woman that is the night. (Gauḍavaho 1166) [Āryā] [p.
