The sky, kissed by the orb of the moon whose light has faded in the middle due to its position in the heavens, resembles a cluster of frogs with their broad bellies slightly split open; it is first sparse because of the thinness of the stars that have set. (Gauḍavaho 1167) [Āryā meter]
Later, as it is being piled up again, the planet Mars becomes visible once more.

(Gaüḍavaho 1168) The expanse of the sky becomes pale with the gradual appearance of the morning light, as if smeared with the essence of twilight that is fading away, reddened by the dawn. (Gaüḍavaho 1169)

A mass of armor arises, its surface uneven with a pale hue marked by the gaps between the lotus-fibers, its body smooth like that of a lion recently bathed; it attains a deep golden-yellow color through the ascending sequence of the dawn. (Gauḍavaho 1170) [Āryā metre]
Just as bees take the quality of the ripening of specific fruits from the branches, [so do lovers take sleep].
In the twilight of the night, they awaken with great difficulty and languidly, their heavy sleep having been obtained for a mere moment during the exhaustion of the exertion of amorous passion.

The mass of seeds from the *gahapalāśī* tree, which has thin roots and emits the glow of a cow’s udder as it is cast off by those following the Tamāla iron-smelting furnace, is later gathered into a heap at night. (Gauḍavaho 1173) [Āryā;
In the bedchambers, the morning breeze, as if grasping her hair, fans the smoke from the lamps that flicker with the tips of their soot-stained crests;
meanwhile, the sky, once soiled by darkness, has become struck by the glow of the dawn. (Gauḍavaho 1174) [Āryā]
Like lead, it has attained its final transformation through the state of vermilion.
(Gaüḍavaho 1175) Due to the influence of the waters of the night, they somehow take up seeds that are harsh to the throat and heavy with the deposition of dust clinging to the wind.
(Gaüḍavaho 1176)

The ponds, with their pairs of cakravāka birds standing in the water, shine as if their eyes were reddened by weeping out of grief for the night-lotuses languishing in the darkness; so too does the moon appear as it descends toward the surface of the western mountain’s peak. (Gauḍavaho 1177) [Āryā]
The moonlight of his fame shines forth, pale and thin like the essence of the nectar of the *sahakāra* tree.
(Gaüḍavaho 1178) The destruction of that [enemy], which proclaims the virtuous conduct of noble men who have endured pure hardships, rends the heart like the discordant age of Kali. (Gaüḍavaho 1179)

The expanse of the sky became pale-red with the *jāyājaya* and *javā* flowers, as if split apart by the radiance of the jewels in the celestial chariots of the immortals who had gathered out of curiosity. (Gauḍavaho 1180) [Āryā;
The first flush of the dawn’s red glow emerges from the sky-king, whose pale star-like petals have withered, possessing the beauty of fresh sprouts;
it flashes forth, radiating a reddish luster like powdered brick-dust.
The orb of the sun, resembling the wheel of the thunderbolt in the sky,
has uprooted that darkness— which was like the ocean’s return due to its density— as if to ensure it never returns again. (Gauḍavaho 1182–1183)
Only when the duties of the night had been completed and he was at ease did he begin to narrate the life-story of Cāṇakya.
[Gaüḍavaha 1184] (In verses) where the lofty and vast [spaces] were purified by the falling chisel-stroke of the iron of darkness...
As if fixed upon walls of hope suitable for the praise of kings,
or like auspicious jars with green sprouts of horses placed at their tops, the solar disc was instantly raised in the eastern quarter. (Gauḍavaho 1185–1186)

While the celestial beauties, their hearts agitated by the desire for their lovers upon hearing the fame of the Lord, were moving about in haste after having been shaken, [the drum] resounded. (Gauḍavaho 1187) [Āryā;

As the avenues of the gardens in the palace of the Lord of the Gods became sparse, with the sprouts of the jeweled crowns of the *asura*s being stripped away by the showers of flowers; [Gaüḍavaha 1188,
Āryā meter] while the air resounded with the sweet warbling of cuckoos whose throats were thrilled by the nectar of the *amr̥ta* tree.
When the mass of auspicious clouds had ascended the expanse of the sky,

the assembly of sages— bound by the longing of Kṛṣṇa and others and moved by haste— seemed as if they had accepted the feet of the celestial deer (the moon) who had come to the heavens out of curiosity. (Gauḍavaho 1189–1190)
The flocks of birds, having abandoned their attachment to trees as if out of curiosity to hear the history of the king composed by Viṇayāḍhatta,
were rendered homeless by the crush of people moving about the hanging great mirrors. (Gauḍavaho 1191) [Āryā]
As the people climbed toward the peaks of the rows of palace pillars,

the surface of the sky became like a gallery constructed upon the lofty palace of the Lord’s white fame, wherein the circles of the celestial chariots of the gods were suspended as if on lotuses. (Gauḍavaho 1192–1193)
Moreover:

Your sword, with its pearl-ornaments consisting of the ichor dripping from the elephants it has captured, triumphs like a necklace formed by the strings of pearls clinging to the necks of the kings of Gauḍa whom it has severed. (Gaüḍavaho 1194) [Āryā]

As if wiping their own feet with the feet of their enemies— who have come here with services rendered out of respect for their equal birth— their feet now move about, stained with blood. (Gaüḍavaho 1195) [Āryā]
O King, you shine on that day with the water of your gifts,
as if by the outpouring of the ocean of the essence of compassion that has filled your heart.
The quarters of the earth, including the oceans, rejoice when you have returned victorious after having conquered them.
Fortune is once again bestowed by you, as if her wealth had been granted by her father through a fresh marriage.

(Gauḍavaho 1197) With feet marked by the stains of fetters experienced for the first time in prisons, your enemies are being cut down by you, as if their life-threads had already been spun out. (Gauḍavaho 1198)
Now, at your prostrations, the brow of your enemy does not rise toward your forehead, as if afraid of being soiled by the dust transferred from the earth.
It seems as if it has been thinned by the repeated mounting upon the shoulders of elephants intoxicated with rut. (Gauḍavaho 1199) [Āryā]
Your elephant, naturally majestic, shines with the grace of its thighs.

(Gaüḍavaho 1200) Because you honor yourself with such pride in your virtues that even those devoid of virtue perceive you as virtuous, for that very reason you consider yourself to possess virtues that are not truly yours. (Gaüḍavaho 1201)
At the very moment you extend your hand to cover the slope of her feet, O Lakṣmī, the daughter of the ocean, at that very moment she passes over to him. (Gauḍavaho 1202) [Āryā meter]
In the expansive, unbroken, and slender rays of your stainless glory, the tresses of the wives of your enemies appear as if reflected in mirrors.
Now, for those whose royal virtues are manifest and directly perceived... [Gaüḍavaho 1203] (Āryā metre)

Even in the opening of the *Vivarana*, there are dialogues intended to awaken the intellect of the lady (*jāyā*). Furthermore: "Now, when it is pure and reddened by the luster of ornaments made of refined gold... (*Gaüḍavaho* 1204, in the Āryā meter).
And also: "Then, when it was pure and dyed crimson by the glow of ornaments of polished gold... (*Gaüḍavaho* 1204).

On that day celebrated by the people, as if made of gold, the world was filled with curiosity; it seemed as though the entire essence of Sarasvatī had descended into him, or as if he were drawn there by the power of his birth. (Gauḍavaho 1205–1206)
Moreover:

Having gained their confidence, she has, as it were, cast out the fortunes of her enemies by the very fault of the treacherous nature of women, and bestowed them upon her friends. (Gauḍavaho 1207) [Āryā]
Upon whose head of victory the opposing goddesses, with their fresh retinues, shed tears that were intercepted for a moment by chowries raised at that very instant. (Gauḍavaho 1208) [Āryā;
O King, listen to this new and wondrous account of that lord of men, which is both purifying and marvelous from beginning to end.
Thus ends the section on the Gāthās in the *Gauḍavaha* of Vappairāja, whose pen-name is Kairāta-lañchana.
